title: CBG vs CBD: What They Are and How to Use Them
description: You’ve likely read about CBD—one of the most buzzworthy naturally-occurring cannabinoids. But you might not have heard about another cannabinoid that’s gaining popularity: CBG, or cannabigerol.

data.text: You’ve likely read about CBD—one of the most buzzworthy naturally-occurring cannabinoids. But you might not have heard about another cannabinoid that’s gaining popularity: CBG, or cannabigerol. It should be noted that CBG and CBD are not new at all—they’ve existed naturally in the cannabis plant for 30 million years! But because they occur more rarely in cannabis plants, extracting them at scale has been a challenge for cultivators, until recently. CBG-dominant cannabis plants are becoming more widely available for purchase and extraction. Access to high-potency CBG extracts now allows for the addition of CBG to products like edibles, tinctures, concentrates, and topicals.

data.text: What's the difference between CBG and CBD?

CBG and CBD bind to our cannabinoid receptors differently. CBG has similar effects to THC, but their different chemical structures affect how they bind to CB1 and CB2 receptors. Because of this, CBG has similar effects as THC without creating an overwhelming psychoactive reaction.* CBG is considered a minor cannabinoid, because the cannabis plant naturally has more CBD than CBG. Because of this, cannabis usually has higher CBD levels than CBG. High CBG levels in a plant can also indicate to a grower that the plant was cut down prematurely, as the plant wasn’t given enough time to process the CBGA into THCA or CBDA. “CBG is the first cannabinoid that a cannabis plant makes. Typically, the amount of CBG in cannabis plants decreases during the flowering stage of a plant’s life cycle, while the amount of THC or CBD increases.” - Alyssa Krause Recently, CBD has been popping up everywhere: in unregulated CBD shops, street corners, and even gas stations. The Farm Bill, passed by Congress in 2018, legalized the production of hemp and cannabinoids derived from those plants. This created a unique legal loophole that legalized cannabinoids. This also created a market that was unregulated. Whereas every cannabis product that you purchase at Sunnyside is required by law to be lab-tested for dangerous things like pesticides and mold, hemp-derived products from the unregulated market have no such requirements. Lawmakers are finally understanding that hemp-derived cannabinoids are not chemically different from cannabis-derived cannabinoids, and they’re beginning to pass legislation that would close this legal loophole. They will also eventually figure out that cannabis plants produce THCA and not THC; therefore, only having laws restricting THC isn’t meeting their goals. All this to say, be mindful of the shifting legal laws when purchasing cannabis, wherever you are. *Individual results may vary.

data.text: What is CBG?

CBG is a cannabinoid that is naturally created by the cannabis plant. It’s one of more than 100 types of naturally occurring cannabinoids, but it’s unique because it’s the precursor to all other cannabinoids. Before a cannabis plant produces THC or CBD, it produces CBG. More accurately, a plant produces CBGA before it transforms it into THCA and CBDA (the acidic forms of these cannabinoids). This is why CBG is often referred to as the “mother cannabinoid.”
What is a cannabinoid?

The word cannabinoid refers to a class of chemical compounds, regardless of structure or origin, that interact with the endocannabinoid system (ECS) through receptors in the body and brain. When cannabinoids bind to these receptors, we feel the effects.
What is the endocannabinoid system?

Our bodies naturally have endocannabinoid receptors built-in, and when cannabis products bind to them, we feel effects. Those bindings are responsible for why your favorite song sounds may just a little better after consuming cannabis. The discovery of the endocannabinoid system (ECS) allowed scientists to learn how these receptors play a large and important role in regulating many bodily functions. Amazingly, the endocannabinoid system was discovered in 1988, while the cannabinoid CBD was first identified in the 1940s. Further research is needed, but over time scientists have discovered that THC and other cannabinoids can affect the body in a multitude of ways. Two main receptors make up the ECS: CB1 and CB2. CB1 receptors are found throughout the body, but are particularly abundant in certain areas of the brain. CB1 receptors are primarily part of the central nervous system.3 CB2 receptors are also located throughout the body and in certain parts of the brain, but are considered part of the immune system, not the central nervous system.4 How you experience cannabis is the result of  which cannabinoids are interacting with which cannabinoid receptors. While both CBD and CBG interact with the ECS, they can produce similar and unique effects within the body and mind. You might be surprised about CBG’s potential effects and how it differs from, and can even compliment CBD. CBG and CBD bind to our cannabinoid receptors differently. CBG has similar effects to THC, but their different chemical structures affect how they bind to CB1 and CB2 receptors. Because of this, CBG may have similar effects as THC without creating an overwhelming psychoactive reaction.*
What is CBGa?

Cannabigerolic acid is the raw form of CBG. Cannabinoids exist in a raw form prior to decarboxylation, a process where cannabinoids are exposed to heat and converted into an activated form. CBGa is the parent of THCa and CBDa—they get converted to THC and CBD with heat and time.

data.text: What is CBD?

CBD (cannabidiol) is one of the most abundant cannabinoids produced by the cannabis plant. It is now possible to find cannabis flower (not just hemp) that is mostly CBD, with negligible amounts of THC and other psychoactive cannabinoids. Similar to THC, the cannabis plant will first produce CBGA before turning it into CBDA. It also requires heat to turn into CBD. CBD not only has no intoxicating effects, it can also mitigate the intoxicating effects of cannabinoids like THC and CBG. It is often referred to as a “safety blanket” for those that consume too much THC for their comfort level. There isn’t a way to undo how much THC you consume, but you can add CBD in hopes that it helps make the experience more enjoyable. CBD also holds an important place in the history of cannabis legalization. Before CBD-dominant cannabis products were available, the public conversation around cannabis focused on the plant’s intoxicating effects. Even though pro-cannabis groups were arguing for access, the public couldn’t get past the idea of legalizing another intoxicating product. It wasn’t until CBD products started being used that a skeptical public started to soften on their views toward cannabis.
What are the Potential Effects of CBG and CBD?
Potential CBG Effects

When it comes to the benefits of CBG, finding your optimal dosage is going to be your first goal. It’s important to remember that CBG is intoxicating, so if you are planning to use CBG to impact your day-to-day, you want to make sure you find a dosage that allows you to keep your faculties.
Potential CBD Effects

Similar to CBG, CBD may promote a general sense of physical comfort. There are a variety of products that are designed to meet these ends. CBD is not intoxicating, but finding your dosage is still an important part of the process. Even though CBD is not intoxicating, it is still psychoactive in that it has an impact on your brain chemistry. So you should still take it slow and start with a low dosage. Not taking too much is also a good way to save money. CBD has no psychoactive effects.
How to Use CBG and CBD

Consuming CBD and CBG is no different than consuming other cannabinoids. You simply have to find a cannabis product that meets your preferred criteria of consumption method and dosage. CBD products are a lot more common in the current cannabis market, so finding a CBG product that meets your preferred consumption and dosage needs might be more difficult. CBG and CBD can be consumed the same way as THC. These cannabinoids are found in cannabis flower, concentrates, edibles, and topicals. How CBD and CBG are used is less important than understanding why they are used. CBD is a cannabinoid that is relied upon by people that are looking to avoid intoxicating effects and/or lessen the intoxicating effects of other cannabinoids. CBG is psychoactive and relied upon for its unique effects. It can be taken by itself, but it is typically paired with other cannabinoids. Like all cannabinoids, they provide a more robust experience when they are consumed together.
Can I Take CBD and CBG Together?

Yes. There are a variety of products that let you either smoke or digest both CBD and CBG. Like all compounds found in the cannabis plant, each will provide a unique experience, but cannabis provides the most robust experience when multiple compounds are taken together and interact with each other. The Entourage Effect is the term we use to describe the synchronistic relationship between these compounds.
Are CBD and CBG Psychoactive?

Yes. Both cannabinoids are psychoactive; however, they are not both intoxicating. This is an important distinction because many people often think of “psychoactive” and "intoxicating" as interchangeable terms. CBD will have a psychoactive impact on your brain, but it will not intoxicate you like if you were to consume THC. CBG, on the other hand, is both psychoactive and intoxicating and can impair your abilities to navigate the world safely.

Why is CBG harder to find than CBD?

data.text: How to Vape Properly
Knowledge is power when it comes to exploring any type of cannabis product, so we’re here to give you the rundown on vapes

Cannabis vaping has soared in popularity recently and it's easy to see why. Vape pens are portable, require nearly no set up or cleanup, and can be hit quickly and discreetly tucked back into a pocket or bag. You can easily adjust the amount of cannabis you consume and save the rest of the cart for later, making vape pens a really practical method of consumption and as easy as simply pushing a button — sometimes even easier.

Vaping cannabis involves inhaling heated oil, flower or concentrates through a vaporizing device, most often a vape pen. The process of vaping includes heating the contents to a temperature that converts the desirable cannabinoids and terpenes - the compounds found in plant material that provide aroma and flavor - into a vapor.
How to Vape Properly

A lot of what it means to vape properly has to do with your preference. Like with all cannabis products, it's best to start with a small amount and use more as needed. There is no way to un-vape what has been vaped, but you can always take another hit.

It is also important to understand the settings on your vape device. If you have control over the setting, know that the higher the temperature, the thicker the cloud, the hotter the vapor will be, and the more you will consume. Lower temperatures will provide more flavor and a smoother draw.

Storage is also important. Anyone who has experience with cannabis vape carts knows the struggle of a clogged cartridge. Modern advances in cart tech have fixed a lot of these problems, but it's still good practice to make sure you keep your upright and out of extreme temperatures.
How to Use a Vape Pen

Pen vaporizers are the most commonly used type of vaporizer, mainly because they're extremely discreet and easy to use. Some vape pens will require you push a button to activate the heating element, but there are some that simply require you draw on the cart and your inhalation activates the device.

But before you can begin vaping, you need to make sure your vape cart and battery are compatible. The vast majority of vape carts work with a standard 510 thread. Simply screw them into your 510 thread battery and start vaping; however, there are vape carts that use proprietary vaping tech. These carts require specific batteries to work. Make sure you have the correct battery for the cart you purchase. You can also buy a disposable vape pen to avoid this situation entirely.
Will My Vape Cart Fail?

The technology for cannabis vape carts was originally brought over from the e-cigarette world. The e-juice that is used in these vapes is made from propylene glycol and vegetable glycerin. This creates an oil that's thin enough to work with a standard wick system, which draws the e-juice to the heating element of the vape.

Even though its consistency varies based on extraction techniques, cannabis oil is too thick by itself to work with a wick system. Producers started using well systems. In these carts, the oil slowly settles into the heating element with gravity. Cannabis producers often add cannabis derived terpenes to help thin the oil and elevate the flavor. Also... fewer failed carts.
Types of Vapes

Vape pens are the most commonly used vape product, but they're just the tip of the iceberg, and they definitely have their limits. The biggest limitation with using vape pens or carts is the selection. Yes, there is a large selection of carts to choose from, but it will never be as large as the selection of flower and concentrates. Using a vaporizer that was designed to use flower or concentrates gets rid of the limitations imposed by cartridges or vape pens.

If convenience and discretion aren't your primary concern when vaping, here are a few other options you should check out.
Flower Vaporizers

For people that look to avoid using cannabis concentrates altogether, there are vaporizers designed to use cannabis flower. There are both handheld and tabletop sized machines; however, the handheld devices are considerably larger than the standard vape pen.

The heating technology used in these devices are designed like small ovens and can be convection, conduction, or a combination of both. Convection heats the cannabis with hot air, and conduction requires the cannabis to come in contact with a heated element.

Similar to concentrate vaporizers, flower vaporizers will have settings that let you adjust the temperature at which you vape. Simply choose your desired temperature, grind the flower, put the ground cannabis in the chamber, and activate your vaporizer. After the flower is spent, clear the chamber, and you are free to reload.
Tabletop Vaporizers

Tabletop vaporizers are large vaporizers that bring more serious capabilities and capacities. What they lack in portability, they more than make up for in functionality. Most will have the ability to vape both flower and concentrates, but most are primarily used to vape flower. These vaporizers will have more options than vape pens when it comes to their settings.

The cannabis is loaded in the main body of the vaporizer, and most utilize a long straw that lets the consumer draw up the vapor. Some tabletop vaporizers also let you draw the vapor into a bag that inflates or a cup. The consumer can then take the bag or cup with them and use it at another location.
Dab Rigs

Dabbing is deconstructed concentrate vaping. Normally you use a larger dab rig; however, instead of using a flame to light flower, concentrates are vaporized in a variety of ways. For a traditional dag rig, the banger (the area where you'll place your concentrates) is manually heated with a torch to the desired temperature. E-rigs are becoming more popular, as they are a lot more convenient. Some even have an app that lets you pick your desired temperature.

While it's not as convenient as a vape pen, dabbing represents the peak of concentrate vaporization. You can consume a variety of concentrates and choose your exact dosage before consuming.
The Basics on Cannabis Concentrates

The golden oil inside your vape cartridge is the result of a meticulous lab extraction process. To make concentrates, a liquid is derived from reducing plant material down to its most potent parts containing all the good stuff: terpenes, cannabinoids, and flavonoids.

Distillate is a widely available, potent cannabis concentrate created through crude oil extraction methods, where the cannabinoids (THC, CBD, etc.) are separated from the plant matter and reconstituted to achieve specific potencies and formulations. Distillates lack the complex chemistry of the cannabis plant and function more as isolates.

Liquid Live Resin and Live Rosin are crafted from fresh-frozen flower through a gentle extraction process which preserves the full plant profile. The resulting oils deliver superior aroma, potency and flavor compared to distillates. Liquid Live Resin and Live Rosin vape cartridges even fit on the same vape batteries as other vapes.

Oils may come with descriptions of strain names, such as Sour Diesel or Girl Scout Cookies, or with certain reported effects like "energize," "uplift," or "relax".
How to Properly Dose with Your Vape

While there's no "one-size-fits-all" dosage for vaping, finding the right fit for you will depend on a range of factors including body weight and tolerance. Everyone's metabolism and endocannabinoid system is different, which can unique results for each person.

The most common vapes recommend short, quick draws as opposed to a few long ones. Exhale thoroughly as THC and CBD enters your system within seconds of inhaling (no need to hold it in your lungs). Wait a minute or two before inhaling again. If it's your first time, wait 10 minutes in between pulls, and ramp up slowly.

For newer cannabis consumers, vaping may be a good place to start because it only requires small pulls and offers a flavorful option that is ready to go whenever and wherever you are.

*Individual results may vary.

data.text: What is Kief & What to Do With It

Kief is one of the original forms of cannabis concentrate. It’s a collection of trichomes that have been removed from dried cannabis plants through agitation. The trichomes are then separated from the plant material through a sieve or with a piece of metal that has a static charge. The collection of these trichomes is what we call kief.

Kief is one of the original forms of cannabis concentrate. It’s a collection of trichomes that have been removed from dried cannabis plants through agitation. The trichomes are then separated from the plant material through a sieve or with a piece of metal that has a static charge. The collection of these trichomes is what we call kief.

The process of removing the trichomes from the plant material has been refined over the years. More modern techniques include using solvents (butane, propane, CO2) or ice water to remove the trichomes. Kief, however, is a term typically reserved for a collection of trichomes that has been collected through a screen or sieve. It does not produce a product that is as pure as modern techniques—there is more plant material remaining in the finished product, but it provides a unique form of cannabis concentrate that sits somewhere between flower and water hash.

Trichomes are delicate—especially after the plant has been dried, and they will fall off the plant if they get handled too roughly. As the cannabis flower gets processed to be sold, producers will take every step to ensure their buds get handled with care. The more delicately they can handle their crop, the more trichomes will be preserved on the flower. This is good news for you, and a sign of a skilled cannabis producer. Unfortunately, no matter how delicate a grower might be with their cannabis, inevitably they will lose some trichomes in the process. Having systems in place to collect that fall-off is the easiest way to ensure that producers get everything out of their crop.

Even if a cannabis producer does an incredible job of preserving the trichomes on their buds, the consumer still needs to be mindful that, as they break down their flower for consumption, trichomes will fall off. Breaking apart your flower on a rolling tray will ensure that the trichomes fall somewhere they can be collected, but using a grinder with a kief tray at the bottom is probably the most convenient way to collect them all.
Kief vs Hash

Hash is the result of removing trichcomes heads from the cannabis plant material and pressing them together, with a little bit of heat, to make a smokeable product. In this way, kief is a type of starting material that can be used to make hash. The result is a product that burns more like incense than kief, which combusts immediately.

The flavor of kief is also going to be different from hash. Kief being fresh, unruptured trichomes, is going to offer a fresher flavor that reflects the true essence of the plant. Pressed hash is going to taste different. Not only will it lack the intense smoke that comes from combusting flower, it also begins to change its chemical and flavor profile as it ages.

Charas is another ancient type of hash that is created in a similar fashion. Instead of agitating dried cannabis material and collecting the kief through a screen, the trichomes are collected fresh from living plants by rubbing one’s hands over the flowers. Charas can be thought of as the first kind of live resin—creating a concentrate from fresh trichomes instead of dried.

As the hash-maker works their hands over the plants in the garden, the sticky resin slowly builds up on their hands. Then they rub their hands together to start working the resin together into a single mass. This mass is often rolled into a ball (sometimes called a “temple ball”) before it is stored before consuming.
How to Make Kief

Kief is most commonly collected with a screen that allows trichomes to fall through as the flower gets agitated above. Kief is technically a concentrate, but, when compared to other forms of concentrate, it is not nearly as pure and potent. So it has less popularity, and it is more often used by producers to enhance products, like infused pre-rolls, rather than sold by itself.

All concentrates are the result of removing the trichomes from the rest of the plant material. Kief is created through a mechanical process that often leaves small amounts of plant material behind. This is why kief is sometimes referred to as “pollen,” because it looks like dust and has a light green or yellow color. The less plant material, the more white the kief will look and the more potent it will be.

Modern extraction techniques are more efficient at removing plant material from the mix. This results in a cannabis concentrate that is more pure, with little to no plant material in the finished product. These concentrates can be dabbed (vaporized) or added to a bowl or rolled into a joint. It’s best not to dab kief or pressed hash, as it will leave your banger dirty and hard to clean.

“Bubble hash” is a term that is frequently used for solventless concentrates (water hash) that are pure enough to dab. It was given this name because the concentrate will bubble when it gets heated instead of combusting or smoldering like traditional pressed hash because there are only trichomes present, no plant material.

Here are a few ways to make kief:
Grinder

The easiest way for the average cannabis flower consumer to make kief is to simply buy a grinder that has a kief tray at the bottom. As you grind your cannabis in the main chamber, kief will gradually start to build up in the kief tray as trichomes fall through the sieve.
Kief Box

A kief box has two chambers that are separated by a sieve. To collect kief, you simply load the top chamber with flower, close the lid, and shake it. It functions similarly to a grinder. Instead of grinding the cannabis flower, the cannabis flower is shaken to get the trichomes to fall off. The trichomes find their way through the sieve and separate themselves from the rest of the plant material. It can then be collected and used.
Static

Kief can also be collected with a static charge. Plant material is sifted and/or agitated so the trichomes fall off. A tool (glove, piece of metal, card or paint roller wrapped in parchment paper, etc) is used to collect the trichomes. Trichomes are light and can take on a negative charge. The rest of the plant material is heavy and maintains a different charge than the trichomes. This makes collecting trichomes with static possible. Modern machinery that utilizes this technology can create a very clean and pure product, similar to bubble hash.
What to Do With Kief?

Kief has been traditionally used by consumers to increase the potency of their cannabis flower by adding it to a bowl or a joint. Grab a small spoon or a card to scoop some up and sprinkle some on top of the flower and consume as usual. Producers will sell it as is, but they will also incorporate it into products like moon rocks or infused pre-rolls.

Moon rocks and joints that get infused with cannabis extract on the outside of the rolling paper would be a sticky mess for the consumer and a nightmare to package for the producer. Dusting the concentrate-dowsed flower and pre-roll with kief is a great way to both up the potency and make it less messy to package and handle.
Conclusion

Kief is a great option if you enjoy smoking cannabis flower and want to increase the potency. Yes, you can add other cannabis concentrates to your flower before smoking it; however, they have a different consistency and burn differently. This can make them difficult to consume. Kief will combust like flower, but hits harder in terms of effects.

Trichomes hold all the magic that makes cannabis cannabis. The unique chemistry of each strain is found in the trichomes. The kief from your favorite strain will give you the same effects as smoking the flower, and mixing that kief with a different flower will give you something new and exciting. Enjoy!

description: As we begin to understand cannabis more and more, many compounds within the plant are gaining attention for their unique properties. One of those is Tetrahydrocannabivarin (THCv).

data.text: As we begin to understand cannabis more and more, many compounds within the plant are gaining attention for their unique properties. One of those is Tetrahydrocannabivarin (THCv). While THC and CBD are the major cannabinoids you've probably heard of, there are many minor cannabinoids like THCv that can play a pivotal role in the body and mind. THCv is a non-psychoactive (which means that in lower doses, it won't create an intoxicating effect) minor cannabinoid (which is a naturally occurring compound in cannabis that are present in smaller amounts versus major cannabinoids). We'll delve into what THCv is, how it differs from THC, and its potential benefits.
How is THCv produced?

Many cannabinoids, including THC and CBD, are produced via the precursor, cannabigerolic acid (CBGA). CBGA is formed as a result of the reaction between the two compounds, olivetolic acid and geranyl pyrophosphate. However, THCv is formed in a slightly different pathway. Instead of reacting with olivetolic acid, geranyl pyrophosphate reacts with divarinolic acid, a molecule that is very similar but has two carbon atoms fewer. This reaction leads to the formation of cannabigerovarinic acid (CBGVA), which then reacts with an enzyme called THCv synthase to form tetrahydrocannabivarin carboxylic acid (THCVA). THCVA is then broken down into THCv via the exact same decarboxylation process (which essentially means exposure to heat) that THCA undergoes to produce THC. We have a blog about that too if you're curious!
Understanding THC vs THCv

THCv is a cannabinoid normally found in sativa strains that interacts with our endocannabinoid systems (ECS) differently than THC does. Let's understand how both of these work at a molecular level. Within the ECS, THC is a weak partial agonist (meaning it stimulates) of both CB1 and CB2 receptors in our brains and produces the psychoactive experience of "being high", while THCv acts as an antagonist (meaning it reduces) of CB1 receptors and a partial agonist of CB2 receptors. Simply put, THCv can counteract some of the psychoactive effects of THC, while also engaging with the ECS in ways that could potentially have some beneficial effects.

What is THCv?
Tetrahydrocannabivarin (THCv) is a cannabinoid normally found in the cannabis sativa plant.
How does THCv differ from THC?
THCv is non-psychoactive and may even counteract some of the psychoactive effects of THC, while also engaging with the ECS.
Does THCv get you "high"?

Simply put, no. In abnormally large doses, THCv can provide some psychoactive effects but this is unlikely to happen in your day-to-day consumption. In fact, THCv may potentially be able to reduce some of the sensation of "being high".
Is THCv legal?
The legality of THCv varies by jurisdiction. Always check local cannabis laws and regulations.
Can THCv be detected in drug tests?
Simply put, yes. A urine test will reveal the presence of THCv.
How can I ensure the quality and safety of THCv products?

To ensure quality and safety, purchase THCv products from reputable sources that provide third-party lab testing. This testing should confirm the product's purity, potency, and absence of contaminants such as pesticides, heavy metals, and mold.
What should I look for when buying THCv products?
Look for: – Third-party lab test results. – Clear labeling of THCv content. – Information on sourcing and extraction methods. – Positive customer reviews and a good reputation.

data.text: Pride Shines Brighter at Sunnyside

Celebrate Pride with Sunnyside! This month we want to highlight the amazing LGBTQIA+ activists who helped pave the way for the legal cannabis experience we enjoy today. Pride is rooted in community, activism, and showing up for one another.

Pride is rooted in community, activism, and showing up for one another.

There's a deep intersection between the fight for LGBTQ+ rights and the movement for cannabis reform — both shaped by people who have been historically marginalized, including queer communities, people of color, and those impacted by criminalization. The progress we see today is built on that shared history of advocacy and resistance.

At Sunnyside, that connection is something we recognize year-round — in our stores, through our teams and in the communities we are a part of.
How We're Showing Up

This month, we're focusing that commitment through both company-wide donations and accepting donations in-store. We'll be contributing to The Trevor Project, Philadelphia Voices of Pride, and the Persad Center Pittsburgh.

Sunnyside locations in Massachusetts, New York, and Ohio will be matching donations up to $4,000 to The Trevor Project. Sunnyside locations in the east of Pennsylvania will be matching donations up to $3,000 for Philadelphia Voices of Pride. Sunnyside locations in the west of Pennsylvania will be matching donations up to $3,000 for the Persad Center Pittsburgh.
Get Involved

If you'd like to take part, you can learn more about the work The Trevor Project, Philadelphia Voices of Pride, or Persad Center Pittsburgh is doing, ask your local store about the organization they're supporting and how you can get involved. Participating states include: MA, NY, OH and PA.
A Shared History of Advocacy
This work is rooted in a much longer history — one shaped by LGBTQIA+ activists whose efforts helped define both the fight for equality and the path to cannabis legalization.
Legal Cannabis Wouldn't Exist without LGBTQIA+ Activists

The path to cannabis legalization has been long forged by activists within the LGBTQIA+ community.

Today, visiting a licensed cannabis dispensary to pick up your flower, concentrates, and edibles is a stark contrast to the experience of visiting the original San Francisco Cannabis Buyers Club, opened in 1992 out of a humble Castro District apartment.

Back then, before cannabis legalization of any kind, it was LGBTQIA+ figures who were pushing the hardest to destigmatize medical marijuana and open legal access for AIDS patients who sought any potential relief they could find.

In fact, without these LGBTQIA+ activists playing an integral role in the evolution of medical cannabis, it's highly likely we wouldn't have legal cannabis today.
Marsha P. Johnson: Pride Origins and Cannabis

The origins of the modern PRIDE movement can be traced back to the work of activists like Marsha P. Johnson, a Black, trans rights advocate and drag queen who was a fixture in New York City's gay arts scene in the 1960's and 70's.

On the night of June 28, 1969, police raided the Stonewall Inn, targeting the LGBTQIA+ community, demanding IDs, beating them with batons, and arresting those who showed resistance. Sparking the pushback, Johnson fired the "shot glass heard round the world" at a mirror screaming, "I got my civil rights," according to Stonewall: The Riots That Sparked the Gay Revolution. In the wake of The Stonewall Uprising and days of demonstrations that ensued, Johnson would become one of the founding members of the Gay Liberation Front and a leading participant in the first Christopher Street Liberation Pride rally on the rebellion's anniversary in June 1970.
Dennis Peron: Legal Forefather

It’s impossible to tell the story of cannabis legalization without acknowledging the tireless effort of iconic activist Dennis Peron, widely regarded as “the father of medical marijuana.”

A Bronx native and Vietnam War veteran, Peron relocated to San Francisco in 1969, after completing a stint with the United States Air Force. He returned stateside with two pounds of cannabis and would go on to sell strains from storefronts in the historically gay Castro District throughout the 1970s. 

As the AIDS crisis ravaged the Castro, the neighborhood became a home base for AIDS patients and activists alike. Peron’s partner, Jonathan West, succumbed to AIDS in 1990 and from there Peron had a clear mission to change the laws criminalizing cannabis possession. He told the Los Angeles Times: “In my pain, I decided to leave Jonathan a legacy of love. I made it my moral pursuit to let everyone know about Jonathan’s life, his death, and his use of marijuana and how it gave him dignity in his final days.” 

Peron worked with a group of activists to author Proposition P, a ballot initiative that recommended California add cannabis to its list of approved medicines to treat various illnesses including AIDS, cancer, multiple sclerosis, and glaucoma, as well as not penalizing doctors for prescribing the medication. The initiative passed overwhelmingly in 1991, and that same year Peron opened the San Francisco Cannabis Buyers’ Club, a medical dispensary that was initially intended for AIDS and cancer patients, but was soon adopted by a variety of seriously ill patients.

That legal cannabis movement continued to blossom with a major victory in the passage of Proposition 215 in 1996, which Peron conceived and co-authored with efforts of friends and activists. Known as the Compassionate Use Act, it exempts patients and defined caregivers who possess or cultivate marijuana for medical treatment recommended by a physician from prohibitive criminal laws. Peron would see his light of compassion shine a path forward for patients up until his death in 2018.
Mary Rathbun: Baker Extraordinaire

Brownie Mary was a feisty IHOP waitress in San Francisco who ran a side hustle selling pot brownies and eventually—despite numerous arrests and raids—used her social security checks to bake 600 brownies a day for AIDS patients.

Beginning in 1984, Mary volunteered at the AIDS ward of San Francisco General Hospital, and later would steer patients to the Cannabis Buyers Club.
Dr. Donald Abrams: Groundbreaking Researcher

Dr. Donald Abrams, an integrative oncologist at the University of San Francisco, was one of the first researchers in the 90’s to study the interaction between cannabis and AIDS.

His research found that cannabis was a safe and effective treatment for AIDS patients, reducing the disease's progression against the immune system, thereby demonstrating its potential medicinal benefits.
Valerie Corral: Advocate & Activist

Santa Cruz activist Valerie Corral, the founder of the Wo/Men's Alliance for Medical Marijuana, a non-profit medicinal cannabis dispensing collective.

After injuries from a car crash, she began using cannabis to curb her seizures, she replaced her 15-pill-a-day regimen and hasn’t suffered a full-blown seizure since. She has become a nationally renowned medical cannabis activist and was a key author of California's Compassionate Use Act.
Paul Scott: Access Advocate

A descendant from Peron's advocacy tree, Paul Scott operated the Inglewood Wellness Center, a medical marijuana collective from 1999 to 2013. 

Similar to the San Francisco Buyers Club, this collective helped AIDS and cancer patients gain access to medical cannabis. 

Scott also founded the Oakland Cannabis Buyers' Cooperative and was the Los Angeles County Commissioner on HIV and AIDS from 2002 to 2008.
Laganja Estranja: Icon & Activist

Transgender drag queen and choreographer, Laganja Estranja (Jay Jackson), utilizes her art to promote the union between cannabis and the LGBTQIA+ community. A Ru Paul’s Drag Race contestant who has written songs like “Look at Me” which stood against arrests for cannabis possession. Laganja is also the creator of cannabis products celebrating PRIDE with the Hepburns pre-rolls, Fruit Slabs infused real-fruit squares, and her own cannabis-centric clothing collection. 

She has been featured on Leafly’s podcast The Hash covering topics like homophobia in the cannabis industry, as well as High Times and on the cover of Dope magazine, making her the first LGBTQIA+ entertainer to be on the cover of a cannabis magazine.
Pride and Cannabis Today

The work of Dennis Peron and his many disciples has resonated throughout the decades and it's quite easy to see how LGBTQIA+ rights and cannabis legalization have become so strongly interwoven — movements that have emerged from marginalized subcultures thanks to citizens and patients turned activists.

Today, same-sex marriage is legal in all 50 states, medical cannabis is legal in 39 states, and recreational cannabis is legal in 24 states. To us, Pride means championing the people who paved the way for us to pursue full-spectrum love and wellness.
Ways to Support

If you'd like to take part, you can learn more about the work The Trevor Project is doing, ask your local store about the organization they're supporting, or simply round up your purchase in-store to donate.

Supporting LGBTQIA+ communities can also take many forms-whether that's contributing to organizations, learnina more about the issues that imoact these communities, or uplifting the people and businesses shaping them today.

title: What is THCa?
description: THCa, or tetrahydrocannabinolic acid is a cannabinoid found in raw & live cannabis plants. It doesn't produce the "high" typically associated with cannabis.

data.text: In the ever-evolving landscape of cannabis usage, cannabinoids besides THC and CBD are starting to gain attention for their unique properties. Cannabis plants produce hundreds of different compounds , and they each contribute something special to the cannabis experience. One such compound is a cannabinoid called THCa (tetrahydrocannabinolic acid). Like all cannabinoids, CBGa is the precursor to THCa. This is why CBGa is often referred to as the “mother cannabinoid.” As a plant grows, instead of producing each cannabinoid individually, it produces CBGa first and then works on transforming that CBGa into other cannabinoids like THCa and CBDa.
What’s the Difference Between THCa and THC?

THCa is the natural occurring, acidic form of THC and is not psychoactive in its natural state. In other words, cannabis plants do not create THC. They create THCa — a compound that will become THC, given the proper conditions. This is why consuming raw cannabis, rich in THCa, will not produce the "high" typically associated with cannabis. THCa and THC also differ in how they interact with your body. THCa doesn’t have the ability to bind to the CB receptors in your endocannabinoid system. It’s only after THCa turns into THC that your body has the ability to tap into the potential effects that may be associated with THC. The information we have about how THCa interacts with the body is extremely limited, but we know from the experiences that it differs greatly from THC.

data.text: What is Decarboxylation?

Decarboxylation is a chemical reaction that removes a carboxyl group from a molecule. In the case of THCa, this process is usually triggered by heat. When cannabis is smoked, vaporized, or cooked, the heat causes THCa to lose its carboxyl group, transforming it into THC. This transformation is why heated cannabis products are psychoactive, while raw cannabis is not. Decarbing your cannabis is an important process to master if you plan to make your own cannabis products at home. It’s possible to buy cannabis oils that have already been activated with heat. Distillate and RSO cannabis oils are created by using heat; therefore, the end result is a cannabis oil that’s already decarbed. Making topicals, tinctures, or edibles from raw THCa plant material requires you heat up the material first if you want a psychoactive experience. THCa converts to THC between 220 and 245 degrees Fahrenheit. It’s important to find a safe and reliable way to keep the temperature in this range. If you go too low, you won’t activate the THCa. If you go too high, you will cook off the THC.
What Does THCa Do?

Most of the time when people buy THCa, they’re intending to turn it into THC through smoking or vaping; however, there’s a growing group of people that ingest THCa. The research around THCa is limited, but there are a lot of anecdotal accounts that speak to the potential of THCa.
The Potential of THCa

Some studies indicate that THCa may encourage cognitive health.* (2)
THCa may help promote a settled stomach.* (3)

items: THCa Isolate: In many ways, this is a pure form of kief. It looks like a white powder and, like kief, can be used to add potency to your flower or concentrate. The trick is isolating the THCa without using heat, which would turn it into THC.

THCa Diamonds: Technically the same as THCa isolate; however, instead of being a powder, it’s in crystal form. They’re created by using specific processing techniques that are more labor intensive. They’re often added to concentrates to improve appearance and increase potency.

THCa Flower: All cannabis flower is THCa flower. Flower will only test positive for THC if it’s been heated and/or degraded somehow. This represents a unique legal loophole for producers, as most laws are written to prohibit THC. This is why it is sometimes legal to buy consumable THCa products through the mail. These products do not become illegal until they are decarbed. All the legal liability for possession of THC resides with the consumer. So, be mindful when purchasing these products (if you live somewhere that allows their sale).

data.text: In today's fast-paced world, quality sleep often seems like a luxury. With adults needing a recommended 7 hours of sleep per night, it's concerning that over a third of adults fall short of this target (1,2). As sleep becomes an elusive necessity for many, the search for effective ways to support restful sleep intensifies. Among the myriad of products flooding the market, Cannabinol (CBN) has emerged as a potential aid. But what exactly is CBN, and can it truly help promote better rest and relaxation? Let's delve deeper into the science behind CBN, explore available products, and understand how they might contribute to better rest.
What is CBN?

While THC and CBD hog the spotlight in discussions about cannabinoids , another naturally occurring compound, Cannabinol (CBN), has quietly gained attention. CBN is a byproduct of the aging cannabis plant. More specifically, as THC breaks down, it converts to CBN. Like its cannabinoid counterparts, CBN interacts with the body's endocannabinoid receptors, impacting functions such as appetite, physical comfort, and mood balance (3). As the demand for sleep aids rises, cannabis companies are incorporating CBN into various products like gummies, capsules, and tinctures, offering potential support for rest and relaxation.
What Does CBN Do?
CBN's interaction with the body's endocannabinoid system is believed to influence central nervous svstem functions (4).

While research on CBN lags behind research on THC and CBD , some studies suggest its potential to promote better rest, particularly when combined with other cannabis compounds and terpenes (5,6). The cannabis plant produces hundreds of compounds, and each compound may work optimally when kept alongside the other compounds (7). This is often referred to as the Entourage Effect.

Unlike THC, CBN is considered minimally psychoactive, meaning users may not experience the typical "high" associated with cannabis consumption. Similar to CBD, the CBN experience is often described by people as what they don't feel. Further research is needed to fully understand CBN's effects on rest, relaxation, and overall wellness.
CBN vs. CBD: What's the Difference?

data.alt: CBN vs CBD: what's the difference?

data.text: Although CBN and CBD share origins in the cannabis plant and interact with the endocannabinoid system, their effects diverge (8, 9). CBN forms as THC degrades, while CBD derives from Cannabidiolic acid (CBDA). Legally, CBD enjoys broader acceptance due to the 2018 Farm Bill, which permits its use if THC content remains below 0.3% (10).

Conversely, CBN products, often containing THC, face stricter regulations. Despite similarities, CBN products tend to be costlier and more challenging to isolate due to their lower abundance in live cannabis plants and the amount of time it takes for THC to actually degrade (it's not fast).
CBN and Sleep: Exploring the Connection

Research on CBN's potential role in promoting restful sleep is ongoing but promising. Some studies suggest that CBN may enhance sleep quality when combined with THC, potentially aiding those seeking better rest (11). However, conclusive evidence on CBN's specific contributions to sleep support remains elusive, necessitating further scientific inquiry. As with any health-related concern, consulting a healthcare professional is essential before considering CBN or any other wellness product.
How Can I Use CBN?

CBN is available in various forms, including gummies , vapes, oils, tinctures, and capsules, catering to diverse consumer preferences. Determining the most suitable product requires consideration of factors such as preferred consumption method, dosage, onset time, and personal health considerations. It is also important to understand that CBN is typically found in products with other cannabinoids. This means finding your ideal balance of CBN, as well as other cannabinoids.

title: What Are Terpenes and Why Do They Matter?
description: There are over 400 different kinds of terpenes within the cannabis plant, and each plant is going to have its own unique fingerprint of aroma. If you’ve ever peeled an orange or plucked some lavender, then you’re already acutely aware of the fragrant oils known as terpenes: they're responsible for the flavor and aroma of your favorite cannabis strain.

data.text: Let's explore one of the most important elements of your cannabis experience—terpenes.

What's cool about these fragrant compounds is that they're not only responsible for the aromas of your favorite cannabis cultivars, but they also play a crucial role in the effects that come with its consumption.
Let's take a closer look so you can get the most out of your cannabis.
What Are Terpenes?

If you’ve ever peeled an orange or plucked some lavender, then you’re already acutely aware of the fragrant oils known as terpenes: they're responsible for the flavor and aroma of your favorite cannabis strain.

These aromatic hydrocarbons are a primary contributor to the distinctive scents and flavors exhibited by cannabis plants. When you smell citrus, floral, pine, or earth in your cannabis, you’re smelling terpenes. They're the reason people love popping a jar of cannabis and sticking their nose in. They make cannabis loud!

There are over 400 different kinds of terpenes within the cannabis plant, and each plant is going to have its own unique fingerprint of aroma. Each plant’s perfume is the result of its genetics, the environment in which it was grown, and the growing practices used by the cultivator. In other words, you can have two plants that are genetically identical and get different terpene profiles if they're grown in different locations and/or were grown with different farming practices.
What Do Terpenes Do?

Terpenes serve as a defense mechanism against predators, help the plant fight off disease, and help the plant attract pollinators. A flower that’s jam-packed with terpenes (a natural solvent) is going to smell amazing, but an animal that’s  looking for a tasty snack may not find it so appetizing. Thankfully, us humans have figured out a way to enjoy cannabis that doesn’t involve eating raw buds.

What this also means is that stress plays a role in terpene production. A plant that's growing in a pristine environment won’t need as beefy a defense system as a plant that's facing more challenges. This is why many indoor growers will intentionally introduce minor stressors to their plants that mimic the stress they would encounter in nature—more terpenes! Each plant will respond differently to different stressors, and a great cannabis product is the result of a producer understanding how to get their cannabis genetics to reach their optimum potential.

When it comes to human consumption, terpenes add to the overall enjoyment of the plant. They're highly volatile, which means they will evaporate at room temperature—giving us a sneak-peek into what we are about to consume. When combusted and inhaled, terpenes will not only contribute to the product's flavor profile, but they'll also have a dramatic impact on the overall experience of the cannabis.

Indica and Sativa are the words that many people use to distinguish the difference between cannabis products. Indica is associated with products that may be more relaxing, and Sativa is a label used on products that may be more uplifting. Whichever you prefer, the terpene profile of the product is going to play a major role in creating that effect. Here’s a closer look at some of the most common terpenes in cannabis products today!
What Are Terpenes In Weed?

Embarking on an exploration of the world of terpenes unravels a tapestry of aromatic compounds, each playing a role in shaping the cannabis experience. Beyond their enticing aroma, these terpenes significantly influence the effects associated with various strains. Let's delve into a more detailed examination of the most common terpenes found in cannabis:

Myrcene: The most common terpene in cannabis. Myrcene commands attention with its musky, earthy scent. Often regarded as the calming force in cannabis, strains that are heavy in myrcene typically offer more sleepy effects—making them an ideal choice for those looking to unwind at the end of the day. Beyond cannabis, myrcene imparts its aromatic charm to hops (a genetic cousin of cannabis), mangoes, and thyme.

Limonene: If your cannabis strain boasts a citrusy kick reminiscent of lemons, limonene is likely the culprit. This terpene brings a burst of sunshine to the aroma and is associated with more uplifting strains.  Limonene's cheerful presence extends to citrus fruits, rosemary, and juniper.

Caryophyllene: For those with a penchant for spice, caryophyllene is the terpene of choice. Delivering a peppery aroma, it stands out in the cannabis world. What sets caryophyllene apart is its interaction with CB2 receptors in the endocannabinoid system. Strains that are high in caryophyllene typically produce a nice body buzz. Caryophyllene's warmth is palpable in black pepper, cloves, and cinnamon.

Pinene: Evoking the crisp, invigorating scent of a pine forest, pinene is a terpene that adds a refreshing touch to your cannabis experience. Apart from its fragrance, strains that are high in pinene offer a more clear experience—making pinene rich strains ideal for when you need to get things done. Also found in pine needles, rosemary, and basil.

Terpinolene: A common terpene that is rarely found in large amounts, terpinolene contributes a sweet, floral, and herbal fragrance to the cannabis bouquet that will remind you of tropical fruit. Strains with significant terpinolene are typically more relaxing. Its presence extends beyond cannabis, making appearances in apples, cumin, and lilacs.

Linalool: Another terpene that’s typically only found in small amounts, linalool introduces a delicate, lavender-like aroma to certain cannabis strains. Known for its relaxing properties, strains that are high in linalool may offer another great option for people looking to increase rest and relaxation. Beyond cannabis, linalool is a common presence in lavender, mint, and coriander.

Humulene: Responsible for the earthy, woody, and spicy aroma in cannabis, humulene is another minor cannabinoid that you can often find in the background. Similar to other terpenes, humulene may support the body's natural recovery processes and help maintain balance and comfort*. (7) Humulene is also found in hops, sage, and ginseng. Humulene is commonly found in strains that are more relaxing in nature.

Ocimene: This terpene provides a sweet and citrusy aroma that will remind you of tropical fruits. Ocimene is often found in small amounts in strains that have their roots in tropical climates and produce uplifting and easy-going effects in their consumers. Ocimene may support the body's natural recovery processes.* (8) Ocimene can also be found in basil, orchids, and mangoes.
*Individual results may vary.

Understanding these common terpenes is akin to deciphering the intricate balance of a cologne or perfume. The interplay of myrcene's calming notes, limonene's citrusy brightness, pinene's refreshing breeze, terpinolene's sweet complexity, caryophyllene's spicy allure, and linalool's floral elegance collectively shapes the nuanced experiences that different strains offer.

As consumers become more discerning in their cannabis choices, recognizing these terpenes becomes a valuable skill. It allows individuals to tailor their cannabis journey, selecting strains not just based on THC or CBD content but on the aromatic symphony created by these terpenes. Whether seeking relaxation, creativity, or a burst of energy, the common terpenes in cannabis are the invisible architects of a personalized and delightful experience.
Terpenes vs. Cannabinoids

Distinguishing terpenes from cannabinoids is crucial for obtaining a comprehensive understanding of how cannabis will impact your experience. Terpenes are hydrocarbons formed by repeating units of isoprene, which contribute to the plant's aromatic diversity. In contrast, cannabinoids represent a diverse array of chemical compounds unique to the cannabis plant, with notable examples being THC and CBD. Both have an impact on the effects.

Regarding production and location, both terpenes and cannabinoids are synthesized in the sticky hair-like, resin glands of cannabis flowers known as trichomes. There are several different types of trichomes on the surface of the cannabis plant, but it’s the large, resinous glands that densely form on the flower (capitate-sessile trichomes) which house the majority and give your cannabis its sticky texture and frosted look.

Terpenes exhibit high volatility and sensitivity to external factors such as heat. Different consumption methods can affect their release and overall presence in cannabis products. In contrast, cannabinoids are relatively stable compounds, less susceptible to variations in temperature and other environmental factors. In other words, cannabinoids have a long shelf-life, but the terpenes, the compounds that dictate the direction of the effects, will evaporate quickly. Freshness matters when it comes to terpenes!

data.text: What Is The Entourage Effect?

When you consume cannabis, you’re getting more than just THC and a few terpenes. You’re actually consuming hundreds of compounds that are all working together to give you an effect that’s more robust than any single compound could offer on its own. The entourage effect refers to the synergistic interaction between the various compounds present in the plant.

Cannabinoids like THC and CBD interact with the body's endocannabinoid system, and terpenes modulate the effects of cannabinoids by influencing their absorption and activity in the body. In other words, if cannabis was a car, cannabinoids would be the engine and terpenes would be the steering wheel. Which way do you want to go?

The entourage effect underscores the potential value of consuming products that provide a wide variety of cannabinoids and terpenes, but that is easier said than done. Growing a cannabis flower that boasts a complex chemistry is the result of good genetics and good growing practices. In many ways, it defines quality.

In the same way, cannabis concentrates can be graded on how well the plant was processed. The best concentrates are the ones that can mimic the chemistry found in the original plant material. The best concentrates are the result of the best flower. Lower-quality concentrates are the result of inferior-quality flower or great flower that has been poorly processed.
Potential Effects and Side Effects
The FDA hasn't officially recognized cannabis as medicine, and individual responses to cannabis can vary.

On the flip side, cannabis use can be associated with side effects, including impaired coordination, dry mouth, and increased heart rate. The psychoactive effects of THC may uplift your mood, but can also lead to paranoia in some individuals. The impact of cannabis on cognitive function and potential long-term effects remain areas of ongoing exploration by researchers.
Consulting with healthcare professionals is essential for individuals considering cannabis use. Healthcare providers can offer personalized advice based on medications and overall wellness goals.*
Personalizing Your Cannabis Experience

As the landscape surrounding cannabis continues to evolve, you’lll have the opportunity to explore and choose from an increasing variety of strains with distinct terpene profiles. Regardless of the experience you're looking for, understanding the interplay of terpenes and cannabinoids allows you to make more informed choices.

It’s also important to note that a cannabis strain is going to interact with each person differently. All of our endocannabinoid systems are unique, so our experience of each cannabis strain will be unique to the individual. This is why trying different strains and products is so important. Find what you enjoy and ask us for recommendations when you want something new!
Final Thoughts

In the ever-expanding world of cannabis, terpenes are key contributors to the diverse and personalized experiences that consumers seek. Understanding the role of terpenes in the entourage effect provides a more comprehensive view of the potential of the cannabis plant. From the soothing embrace of myrcene to the invigorating notes of limonene, each terpene adds a layer to the cocktail of psychoactive compounds that is cannabis.

As research progresses and the cannabis industry matures, the importance of terpenes in shaping the cannabis landscape becomes increasingly apparent. Consumers are empowered to make choices based not only on cannabinoid content but also on the aromatic nuances that contribute to the enthralling experience of consuming cannabis. They can tailor their experience to specific preferences. As the cannabis industry continues to evolve, with products sold in various forms, this knowledge allows people to explore the vast array of strains and products available, unlocking the full potential of this remarkable plant.

data.text: The "Entourage Effect" is the theory that cannabis is better than the sum of its parts. It argues that when you consume compounds like THC or CBD, they're at their best when accompanied by the other 400+ compounds that are found in the cannabis plant. The idea behind this synergy isn't hard to grasp, but there's been a fundamental lack of communication by the cannabis community to evangelize just how important this idea is for navigating the cannabis landscape. Too often the conversation gets bogged-down in terminology, and too much focus gets placed on the limited research that exists around this highly scheduled product. A quest to understand more about it has been the primary driver of the cannabis community since before cannabis was legalized. It played an important role in bringing legitimacy to the plant in the eyes of the public and paving the way for a legal market; however, it's not the only lens through which we should be viewing cannabis.

data.alt: The Building Blocks of Cannabis: cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids work together to create the Entourage Effect and enhance potential effects.

data.text: A Different Way to Look at Cannabis

For most consumers, the entourage effect is best viewed through the lens of quality. Quality directly speaks to the strength of a product, the price of products, and the variety of experiences those products may provide. Cannabis that offers a complex chemistry is going to cost more because it takes more time to develop and skill to grow, and producers of these products are willing to go through the effort to make them because they create the best experience for the consumer. In other words, we may not have all the scientific studies to completely understand the nuances of the entourage effect and how all the compounds interact with each other. We still haven't figured out all the compounds that are in cannabis, but we do have enough empirical data and expertise in the field to know that quality cannabis, which is partially defined by a complex chemistry, produces the best effects.
Are you Interested in Buying THC, or Buying Cannabis?

A lot of people still don't know what they're buying when they buy cannabis, nor what it takes to create a quality cannabis product. They just want THC, and they are missing out on the best the plant can offer. It's not uncommon for someone to walk into a cannabis shop and simply purchase the product with the highest THC percentage, as if the more THC the better. These buying habits have had a powerful impact on the cannabis market-making it really difficult for quality to survive. The truth is, THC percentage has nothing to do with the quality of a cannabis product. Using THC potency as a distinguishing factor is like walking into a coffee shop and asking for the coffee with the most caffeine. Will that beverage produce an effect when consumed...yes, but so will caffeine pills. Coffee producers and consumers both know that there's more to a nice cup of coffee than caffeine. A great cup of coffee is the result of time and craft. Great cannabis is the same. It takes time to breed a plant that produces a complex chemistry. It takes skill to grow that plant so it can reach its potential. It takes earned wisdom to know when to chop down the plant and how to properly dry, cure, and store the plant so the diverse chemistry sticks around. And it's pure art when an extractor can process all of those compounds (many of which are extremely volatile) into an oil that truly reflects the diversity of the plant from which it came. Making a great cannabis product takes more than just being able to farm THC.

data.text: The Entourage Effect Means More Enjoyment

We may not have the scientific studies to definitively show the full impact of the entourage effect, but we can say some things for sure. Based on what we know about our experiences with cannabis, cannabis is more enjoyable when there is more to it than just THC. It will have an enjoyable aroma and flavor—letting you know that volatile terpenes and flavorants are still around. It will produce a smooth smoke—having avoided the harshness that comes from overly dried and quickly cured cannabis. And the effects will be more robust and last a whole lot longer than if you were to just consume THC by itself. The reality is that it's easy to make THC. It's not volatile, and it doesn't take a lot of effort to find sturdy plants that can yield high numbers (especially when that's the main purpose of the growing operation). Its stable nature also allows it to easily be isolated into oils like distillates and put into vape carts and edibles. This is why it's typically the products that contain the highest levels of THC (distillates) are the more affordable products; however, this is also why people that know cannabis, and are looking for a higher quality product, are buying products that might not have the highest THC percentage. They know that these products, even though they contain a lower THC percentage-may offer better and longer experiences than products of lesser complexity. It's also important to know that between the isolates and full-spectrum products lies a variety of products that speak to the diversity found in the quality of the producers and the type of extraction process used to make concentrates.

data.text: A Word on Concentrates

When it comes to buying quality flower, the first step is finding a good grower that is producing something great. The next step is making sure that the product you're buying was handled with care, so that it didn't degrade before it got to you. Then it's about freshness. From the moment it gets cut down, the plant starts to degrade. Think of it this way...when you're buying cannabis flower, you're buying produce. It has a shelf life, and the shelf life of your cannabis flower is longer if you take care of it by storing it away from light, oxygen, and high temperatures. When you buy quality concentrates, you're buying something that started as pristine flower material, and the perfect concentrate is going to be one that holds onto all of the chemical diversity that was present in the original flower. That's the primary goal of every extraction artist who's investing in making a quality concentrate. However, that isn't the only goal when creating concentrates. There are lots of different kinds of concentrates on the market. The more expensive concentrates cost more because they went through the entire quality process. They had good flower and ended up with an extraction that held onto the chemistry of the plant. It's also important to note that they can be the result of solventless and solvent-based extraction methods. There isn't a singular method that will guarantee quality. It's always dependent on the quality of the original material and the skill of the extraction artist. Quality can be produced from a variety of growing methods and extraction methods. The more affordable options are the result of one or two things. They could be made with lower quality flower, i.e., flower that does not express a complex chemistry or was grown or handled poorly. Secondly, some extraction processes are designed to isolate certain cannabinoids. Distillate is the most popular way to create such an isolate. Heat is used to isolate the cannabinoid of choice. This results in a very clean product (eliminating things like mold on the plant material in the process) that can be produced quickly and efficiently; however, it's also a product that lacks the full entourage effect. The result is a noticeable difference in the experience of the product, when compared to the products with a full chemistry. If you go a little higher on the shelf, you will notice products with mid-level chemical diversity or distillates that have been infused (post-extraction) with terpenes. These man-made terpene profiles are typically designed to mimic the 3 primary terpenes found in the original plant. Other cannabinoids like CBN and CBG are also starting to find their way into these products as well. While this is good for the consumer, keep in mind that it isn't just a handful of compounds that give a strain its luster, it is hundreds. So, while the effort is appreciated, these products will never compare to concentrates that simply held onto the chemistry of the original plant material. It's too complex to copy.
Final Thoughts

There are lots of ways to view the Entourage Effect. Science will offer their insights into the process, but that's just one way to look at it. For the average consumer, a more meaningful way to view it is through the lens of quality. The Entourage Effect is what you're chasing when you're looking for a good cannabis experience. It's what you're paying for when you decide to spend more on a product. Cannabis is hundreds of compounds that are working together to give you an enjoyable experience. Each person is going to have their preferences when it comes to the chemistry of a plant. It's that unique chemistry that defines strains (like a fingerprint) and, therefore, experiences. Quality is something that transcends those differences. You may not love the experience that a particular strain offers, but you can know whether a product offers a quality representation of that strain. You just have to know what to look for. Frequently Asked Questions:
What is the Entourage Effect?

The Entourage Effect is the theory that cannabis compounds, such as cannabinoids and terpenes, work better together than in isolation. This synergy enhances the overall experience and effects of cannabis beyond what a single compound can achieve.
Why is the Entourage Effect important?

The Entourage Effect plays a crucial role in the quality of cannabis products. Rather than focusing solely on THC percentage, consumers should seek products that maintain a diverse and complex chemical profile for richer experiences.
Does higher THC mean better cannabis?

No, THC percentage alone does not determine quality. Great cannabis is defined by complexity, aroma, flavor, and overall experience. The best cannabis products balance multiple compounds to create the desired effects.
What's the difference between full-spectrum and isolated THC products?

Full-spectrum products retain a wide range of cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavorants, offering a well-rounded experience due to the Entourage Effect. Isolated THC products, like distillates, may be potent but lack the depth and complexity of full-spectrum options.
Are infused distillates a good alternative?

Infused distillates, which have added terpenes or other cannabinoids post-extraction, may offer improved experiences over plain THC isolates. However, they cannot fully replicate the natural complexity of full-spectrum extracts.
How should I store my cannabis to maintain quality?

To preserve freshness and potency, store cannabis in a cool, dark place away from light, oxygen, and high temperatures. Proper storage helps maintain the compounds that contribute to the Entourage Effect.

What is microdosing?

In this case, microdosing is using small amounts of cannabis to limit certain effects. It's also an easy, effective route to reintroduce cannabinoids into your system after not using cannabis for a long time. It's important to remember that the "micro" in microdosing is different depending on the person. Anyone relatively new to cannabis may have a very different definition than seasoned users. Let's start with why you might want to go micro.

data.text: How to Go Micro

For what it's worth, we recommend microdosing via edibles, capsules or tinctures. It's a lot easier to manage and these are designed for microdosing. With that in mind, here's an overview of microdosing methods.

Inhalables: Start with a strain with a low THC content. For flower, ideally use a vaporizer, take a hit, hold it in briefly, exhale, and evaluate how you feel after 10 minutes. If you're using a concentrate vape that offers heat settings, ensure it's on the lowest possible. Take a quick puff, hold, exhale, and wait for about 10 minutes. Ingestibles: Edibles and capsules that are anywhere between 1-2.5mg make for a great place to start, plus you can slowly increase the dosage as you see fit. Just remember to be a little patient- edibles can take up to 90 minutes to fully kick in. If you're opting for tinctures, pay special attention to the concentration of the tincture. Most people take 3-5mg per dose. The onset time is not immediate (about 15 minutes), so be sure to wait a bit before taking more.
Getting Started with Microdosing
Microdosing is not an exact science, despite the fancy label. There are many things at play including weight, body chemistry and tolerance level. It's important to keep the following in mind:

In almost all cases, you should start at the lowest possible dose. For most users, this is somewhere around 1mg of THC, 5mg of CBD (which is generally known to help take the psychoactive edge off), and 1-2.5mg for other cannabinoids (like CBN or CBG).
When in doubt, always consult a medical professional. They'll be able to give you a more personalized recommendation based on your goals.

When it comes to microdosing, patience is the name of the game. It might take some time to figure out what dosage and cadence is right for you. Once you've fine-tuned your process, you'll be able to enjoy cannabis at your own pace.

data.text: Cannabis vs Alcohol
Whether you're a regular consumer of either alcohol or cannabis, it's good to know how the two compare and the reasons why it's unwise to mix them together.
Cannabis and Alcohol: How do the two compare?

While your body’s ways of processing cannabis and alcohol are complex, here are the basics. Both cannabis and alcohol are psychoactive—that’s science-talk for a chemical substance that changes your brain function . They alter your perception, mood, and behavior.

How they affect your mind is where alcohol and cannabis diverge. Alcohol is a depressant , meaning it slows down brain functions and neural activity–which can dull your overall perception and can lead to a relaxed feeling as your muscles loosen up. Alcohol also heavily impacts your motor skills via the central nervous system.

Cannabis or, more specifically, the compound THC in cannabis is multifaceted and can have the properties of a depressant (relaxing, sleep-inducing), a stimulant (elevated moods), and can even alter your sense of time and space. While more research needs to be done, cannabis may affect your brain activity and may magnify your thoughts and creativity . (Individual results may vary).
How will I feel the morning after a night of using cannabis vs. alcohol?

When it comes to “the morning after” a night of indulgence, you may continue to feel the effects. These sensations typically don't compare to the discomfort of an alcohol hangover. While THC is a fat-soluble chemical that the body stores after you’ve consumed it, the majority of the noticeable effects of cannabis should be gone within a matter of hours –regardless of the potency of the product. A few examples of lingering effects you might feel the morning after overindulging could be fatigue or dry eyes and mouth.

Compare that to the sensation of waking up after a night filled with a few too many and experiencing stomach pain, nausea, rapid heartbeat and increased sensitivity to light and sound. Also keep in mind that alcohol affects all people differently, and severe alcohol hangovers can linger for several days .
In terms of dosing, what’s the cannabis equivalent to having a serving of alcohol?

The alcohol content ratios between a pint of beer, a shot of liquor, and a glass of wine are common knowledge. But there isn’t quite a direct translation between, say, a pint of beer and a half-gram joint of cannabis. However, any cannabis product you pick up at a licensed dispensary will clearly label the THC:CBD ratios and percentages right on the packaging.

If you’re smoking, vaping, using sublinguals or concentrates, it’s easier to manage the effects by taking smaller hits over a longer span of time. With topicals, you can re-apply as needed. With edibles or transdermals, it’s recommended to wait at least 2-3 hours before trying more since the onset of effects is delayed (individual results may vary).
