description: We'll guide you through the process of accessing a medical card, educate on the many different delivery methods and product forms, and most importantly—point you on a path to help you make decisions to feel your best!

data.text: Navigating Medical Marijuana

We'll guide you through the process of accessing a medical card, educate on the many different delivery methods and product forms, and most importantly—point you on a path to help you make decisions to feel your best!
Navigating Medical Marijuana

What is medical marijuana? You might think that it refers to a special type of cannabis that is different from the recreational kind, but this is not the case. There is nothing inherently different between the cannabis that you find in a medical dispensary and a recreational pot shop. Sure, you will find some small differences in the manufactured products; however, these differences have more to do with the laws that govern the two categories of cannabis than the actual cannabis itself.

Medical marijuana and recreational cannabis are both highly regulated. Customers have strict limits on how much they can purchase, and producers have strict guidelines on the products they can bring to market. The ways they differ are in the way taxes are collected – patients don’t pay taxes at retail - and producers of medical marijuana products have a different set of rules that govern their production line (in states with both types).

When it comes to purchasing, patients with medical cards can avoid paying certain taxes on their cannabis and have the ability to buy more (and have more in their possession) at the point of sale. It is also common for producers to be able to produce more potent products for medical patients—potency levels that would be illegal in recreational markets. In other words, medical marijuana is all about access.
How to Get Access

Each state that offers medical marijuana is going to have their own laws that govern people looking to gain access to this wonderful plant; however, there are similarities in the process. For example, every state is going to have a list of approved medical conditions, and someone looking to get a medical card needs to have a qualified physician’s diagnosis of one of these conditions to qualify. Degrees of approved conditions vary by state, with some states focusing only on severe medical conditions and others open to a wider array of less severe conditions. If you believe you qualify, your condition will need to be verified by a doctor, and that doctor will also need to be willing to sign off on you using cannabis. It sounds simple, but not all doctors are willing to walk through this process, and each state is going to have their own paperwork—some of which can be quite confusing. After you have successfully navigated through all of the medical examinations and paperwork, you are finally in a position to get your medical card and legally purchase medical marijuana. However, your work isn’t done yet!
Where to Get Educated

The “medical” terminology can also be a little misleading because it differs so much from the way we typically get cannabis. When you go to a doctor and need medicine, the doctor will write you a prescription, you take it to the pharmacy, and they give you exactly what you need. You aren’t going to show up to the pharmacy and be able to have your pick. Unfortunately, when it comes to medical marijuana, doctors have the ability to give you access but very few have the experience and/or training to offer guidance on which products to prescribe. Also, instead of a pharmacy, you are directed to a cannabis dispensary, and each dispensary is going to offer different products and have staff with different levels of training. In other words, each patient is going to have to do their own homework when it comes to finding their cannabis and a dispensary that meets their needs. Thankfully, there are dispensaries with excellent staff that are trained to help you find exactly what you need. In fact, you are on one of those dispensary’s websites right now! Before you head out to a shop, here are a few things you should know.
How to Buy
Like with any cannabis you take, you are going to want to know how medical marijuana is going to affect you. Here are a few helpful hints to get you started on your journey.
How Do You Want to Consume?

The first thing you are going to want to do is decide how you want to consume the cannabis. This is about more than your personal preference. How you consume is going to have a profound affect on how you experience the plant's effects. When you inhale smoke or vapor, you are going to feel the effects almost immediately, and you should expect to be enjoying those effects for about two hours. Edibles, on the other hand, can take up to an hour to kick in and can last for six hours or more.

data.alt: person practicing yoga with a cannabis vape pen

data.text: There’s even an option for you if you want something between the two! Tinctures are designed to be absorbed directly into your bloodstream through your mouth. You will typically feel the effects within 15 minutes, or you can use them like an edible and combine it with your favorite food or beverage. Topicals are also a great option if you prefer not to ingest orally. With all these options, you just need to pick the one that is going to work best for you!
How Do You Want to Feel?

Not all medical marijuana is going to make you feel the same way. There are certain products that are going to make you feel more relaxed and there are some that are going to feel more uplifting. Within the world of strain types , ones that are more relaxing are often referred to as “Indica,” and those that are more uplifting are referred to as “Sativa.” “Hybrids” are strains that fall somewhere in between the two. You can even avoid more heavily intoxicating effects if you wish. Products that are high in CBD and low in THC may offer you the effects you are looking for without the high that is often associated with cannabis. Topicals also do not deliver intoxicating effects. These products are ideal for people that use medical marijuana but need to remain unintoxicated.
What’s Your Dosage?

After you have found your products, all that is left to do is figure out your dosage. As the old adage goes, “start low, and take it slow.” You will always be able to take more, but there is no way to remove what you’ve already taken. So if this is your first time consuming, or your first time consuming in a long time, start by taking a small dose. If it’s an edible , start with 2-5 mgs, give it 4 hours, and try to take some more if it isn’t as potent as you like. If it is a product that requires smoking or vaping, take a small inhale and give it thirty minutes before attempting more.
Even though you aren’t going to overdose, you still want to avoid a negative experience (anxiety) because you take too much.
How to Travel With Medical Marijuana?

Don’t. Cannabis is still federally illegal. Airports are on federal land. Your medical card is only valid in the state you got it in. Learn from all the recent news of people getting caught and imprisoned in other countries for trying to bring in their personal stash through foreign airports. Be smart about it!
Final Thoughts

In short, medical marijuana has to do with a person’s ability to access the plant. It’s the same plant you will find in the recreational market, just presented differently. If you are looking into medical marijuana, consult your doctor, do your research, and find a great dispensary you can count on to help you get what you need. We’ll see you soon!

title: Rethinking Alcohol
description: Rethinking alcohol consumption has become a popular trend that has led many people to participate in the Dry January Challenge.

data.text: Rethinking Alcohol
Rethinking alcohol consumption has become a popular trend that has led many people to participate in the Dry January Challenge.

What is Dry January? It's when an adult decides to either reduce or give up their alcohol consumption for one whole month. Many choose to start following the holidays and New Year's or in conjunction with their resolutions to live a healthier lifestyle. There are countless reasons why you might choose to adjust your relationship to alcohol, and there are a myriad of ways in which your goals can be achieved. You can go completely sober, or you can use the challenge as a way to create a healthier connection to alcohol.

Whatever your reason for wanting to participate in Dry January, you may find there are a lot of other factors to consider when choosing to reconsider your relationship with alcohol. One of the biggest involves reimagining the spaces and occasions in which alcohol is just along for the ride.

You can have a glass of wine to round out a meal, you can enjoy a well-crafted cocktail when you’re out with friends, or you can crack open a cold one to unwind after a long day. For many people, it’s not necessarily about needing a drink. It’s about enjoying a moment or finding relaxation.

Unfortunately, the effects of alcohol are not all positive. It certainly takes its toll on your health—leading many to pursue a drier January; however, not drinking alcohol does not mean you also have to give up your favorite moments. You just have to get a little creative with your rituals.

If you are looking for something to replace that alcoholic beverage for Dry January, look no further than cannabis. Like alcohol, cannabis comes in a variety of forms and flavors that are designed to meet your specific needs.

You might even find some company in your new endeavor! A recent study done by New Frontier Data found that, “Among cannabis consumers who also drink alcohol, nearly half (47%) have replaced at least some of their alcohol use with cannabis.”
So, let’s take a closer look at how you can replace your next alcoholic beverage with cannabis!
The Potential Benefits of Cannabis

If discretion is important, edibles and vaping products will be a great place to start. Both can be easily concealed, and neither will produce a loud aroma. If discretion is not a high priority on your list of needs, unwinding with a high-quality joint might be just what you’re looking for.

Unlike alcohol, cannabis can offer a wide spectrum of effects . Some products may produce uplifting effects (Sativa) that are great for social events, and some may potentially produce relaxing effects (Indica) that are perfect for getting nice and relaxed. The list of potential effects is lengthy, but the point is that cannabis products can be curated to meet your needs and enhance your experience.

description: Over 150 different cannabinoids have already been discovered in cannabis, and we are still searching! We'll take a closer look at the different types of cannabinoids prevalent in your favorite products, and how to best tailor them to meet your specific and varied needs.

data.text: What Are Cannabinoids?

Over 150 different cannabinoids have already been discovered in cannabis, and we are still searching! We'll take a closer look at the different types of cannabinoids prevalent in your favorite products, and how to best tailor them to meet your specific and varied needs.
What Are Cannabinoids?

As you might have guessed from the name, cannabinoids play an essential role in the life of the cannabis plant. They are also the compounds responsible for the litany of experiences that result from its ingestion. In short, cannabinoids are compounds that interact with our endocannabinoid system —a biological system that promotes homeostasis in our bodies. It works to keep our bodies performing at an optimal level. In this way, cannabinoids may help with relaxation, and that's one of the primary reasons humans have consumed this plant for thousands of years. But this plant isn’t just making them for us. Cannabinoids play an important role in keeping the plant healthy. Predominantly found in the trichomes of the plant, they help protect the plant from the harmful UV rays from the sun and help ward off pests that are looking for an easy snack. Cannabis plants produce a large amount of cannabinoids; however, cannabinoid production is not just limited to cannabis! Cannabinoids occur naturally within other plants as well as the human body. They can also be created synthetically in a lab. Of the over 150 cannabinoids produced by the cannabis plant, there are only two that show up in large quantities—THC and CBD. Most cannabis products will have a cannabinoid profile that is dominated by these two cannabinoids; however, minor cannabinoids are starting to make an appearance on the market as well! So let’s take a closer look at the different types of cannabinoids, and how we can best utilize them to meet our needs!
The 3 Types of Cannabinoids

Phytocannabinoids are found in plants; however, nothing in the plant kingdom comes close to cannabis when it comes to the quantity and diversity of cannabinoids found therein. Over 150 different cannabinoids have already been discovered in cannabis, and we are still searching! It’s a little misleading to say that cannabis produces cannabinoids. Cannabis plants actually produce cannabinoid acids. In other words, instead of THC and CBD, cannabis produces THCa and CBDa. You might see these on the label of your cannabis products. THCa and CBDa convert to THC and CBD when heat energy is introduced—a process called decarboxylation. This is why we smoke cannabis, and this is why you need to activate cannabis with heat before you eat it. THCa and CBDa are not psychoactive until they undergo this process. Endogenous Cannabinoids are produced naturally within the human body. They are part of our endocannabinoid system and work toward keeping our body in a state of homeostasis. The two main endogenous cannabinoids are anandamide and 2-AG. Endogenous cannabinoids and phytocannabinoids are similar in structures; therefore, phytocannabinoids are able to supplement our endocannabinoid system by binding to the cannabinoid receptors found throughout our bodies. Synthetic Cannabinoids are manufactured in one of two ways. First, they can be made by chemically altering CBD. CBD is legal at the federal level; therefore, chemists do not have issues getting CBD from hemp companies to use as their base for creating synthetic cannabinoids. You can also grow cannabinoids from yeast, bacteria, or algae. Even though these cannabinoids are the same structure as natural occurring cannabinoids, the synthetic label is given to these cannabinoids because they are the result of genetic engineering.
Major vs Minor Cannabinoids in Cannabis
Major Cannabinoids

The two major cannabinoids are THC and CBD . The percentage of these compounds will vary from plant to plant; however, no other cannabinoids come close to these two when it comes to quantity. Both THC and CBD are psychoactive; however, THC is the only cannabinoid that has been proven to be intoxicating. This does not mean that the rest of the compounds have no part in your cannabis experience. THC might be the only intoxicating cannabinoid, but CBD and the other hundreds of compounds in cannabis have an effect on THC’s expression. Many people believe that THC is not very enjoyable by itself, as it has the tendency to produce paranoia. It requires the company of other compounds (cannabinoids and terpenes) to make the experience something special. This is also why many people believe that the synthetic cannabinoids developed to replace traditional cannabis consumption did not work as well as expected. These synthetic cannabinoid compounds were being introduced individually to patients, and, even though they were identical in structure, they could not compete with the hundreds of compounds working together in cannabis products.
Minor Cannabinoids

Two minor cannabinoids that are making their way into products are CBG and CBN. CBGa is actually the first compound that the cannabis plant makes. The plant then synthesizes it into either THCa, CBDa, or CBCa. CBG is similar to CBD in that it doesn’t offer intoxicating effects, while also producing notable effects; however, it differs in the receptors that it binds to in the body. CBN is the result of THC breaking down. Given enough time, and exposure to light and oxygen, THC will break down into CBN. Cannabinoids really are incredible. Even when they break down, they are still useful!

data.alt: person lighting up a cannabis joint

data.text: How We Experience Cannabinoids

Lastly, it is important to point out that how we experience cannabinoids is directly linked to how we consume cannabis products. For example, when we smoke cannabis or inhale from a vape, the effects are felt almost instantly, but when we eat or drink cannabinoids, the onset takes much longer because the cannabinoids must first make their way through your gastrointestinal tract before they are processed by the liver. Eating cannabis is also a very inefficient way to consume cannabinoids. The bioavailability of cannabinoids when smoked is over double when compared to eating; however, considering that edibles and smoking provide very different experiences, and everyone’s endocannabinoid system is unique, it’s really more about finding the method that works best for you! You might just find your new favorite!

title: The Ultimate Guide: Indica vs. Sativa
description: Maybe you’ve seen these terms before, but what do they mean and what can they tell you about the cannabis you’re enjoying?

data.text: Cannabis is a complex plant with a rich history and a variety of uses—ranging from medical to recreational. One of the most common distinctions made within the world of cannabis is between Indica and Sativa strains. These categorical terms have existed since the beginning of the modern cannabis revolution, but their definition has changed over the years and mean different things in different contexts.

These two categories represent different types of cannabis plants that produce distinct effects and grow in unique ways. Whether you’re a seasoned user or a curious newcomer, understanding the differences between Indica and Sativa can enhance your cannabis experience. Here’s what you need to know!
Origins and Botanical Differences
Indica

Origins: Indica cannabis plants are native to northern regions with harsh climates, such as the Hindu Kush mountains of Afghanistan and Pakistan. These plants evolved to withstand colder, mountainous environments, and their characteristics reflect that environment.

Appearance: Indica plants are generally short and bushy, with broad, dark green leaves. They grow to about 3-4 feet tall, making them ideal for indoor cultivation. Since these plants evolved in arid conditions, the trichomes on these plants grow more densely. This helps the flowers retain moisture by providing a covering for the plant material. This also makes them ideal for hash-making.

Growth Cycle: Indica strains tend to have a shorter flowering time, usually between 6 to 8 weeks. Since they grow further away from the equator, they have evolved to handle smaller growing windows. This quick maturation process makes them a popular choice for growers looking for faster harvests.
Sativa
Origins: Cannabis Sativa plants originate from warmer equatorial climates such as Central America, Southeast Asia, and Africa. These regions provide the ideal conditions for Sativa’s growth.

Appearance: Sativa plants are taller and thinner than their Indica counterparts, often reaching heights of up to 20 feet in the wild. They have narrow, light green leaves and a more sparse foliage. Because they grow in humid conditions, the plant structure is more open and the trichomes are less dense (but typically higher in THC) so the plant can get air and avoid mold and mildew.

Growth Cycle: Sativa strains typically have a longer flowering time, ranging from 10 to 16 weeks. This extended growth period is suitable for outdoor cultivation in warm climates with long growing seasons. Longer growing cycles are not ideal for cultivation, as it means cultivators require more time to bring them to market.

data.text: Effects and Uses
Indica
Effects: Indica strains are often associated with relaxing effects. The high produced by Indica strains is often described as a "body high," leading to physical relaxation and a sense of calm.

Common Uses: Due to their calming effects, Indica strains are typically recommended for evening or nighttime use. They are popular among individuals seeking to unwind after a long day. *Individual results may vary.
Popular Strains: Some well-known Indica strains include Northern Lights, Granddaddy Purple, and Afghan.
Sativa

Effects: Sativa strains are known for their uplifting and energizing effects. The high from Sativa strains is described as a "head high," characterized by increased creativity, focus, and sociability.

Common Uses: Sativa strains are usually recommended for daytime use due to their stimulating effects. They are favored by individuals who may be looking to enhance creativity, engage in social activities, or boost their energy levels. *Individual results may vary.
Popular Strains: Popular Sativa strains include Sour Diesel, Jack Herer, and Durban Poison.

data.alt: Infographic comparing the reported effects of indica vs sativa strains

data.text: Hybrid Strains: The Best of Both Worlds

In addition to pure Indica and Sativa strains, there are countless hybrid strains that combine the characteristics of both types. Hybrids are bred to provide a balanced experience and meet the demands that face cannabis farmers. These strains can be Indica-dominant, Sativa-dominant, or balanced—catering to a wide range of preferences and needs.

For cannabis consumers looking to purchase products at dispensaries, “hybrid” is typically going to be used to identify products that offer an effect somewhere between Indica and Sativa. Hybrid strains may offer a mix of relaxation and energy, making them versatile for different situations. They are often chosen for their tailored effects, which can be adjusted by breeders to achieve specific outcomes.
Popular Hybrid Strains: Some popular hybrid strains include Blue Dream, Girl Scout Cookies, and Pineapple Express.
Everything Is Basically A Hybrid

In reality, almost every cannabis product we consume today is a hybrid. A plant may be “Indica” in its effects, but that doesn’t mean that its genetics are exclusively Indica. Pure Indica and Sativa plants (landrace strains) evolved to grow in specific areas of the world, and the plant needs the environment and cultivation practices of that specific area to flourish. In other words, it’s difficult for growers to replicate those environments.

This is why cannabis farmers spend time breeding plants. They are trying to find a plant that will grow well in the conditions they have to work with. They may want the effects of a Sativa, but they need the structure and grow-cycle of an Indica plant. Maybe they are growing somewhere with high humidity, and they need their indica plants to grow a little more open to avoid molding and ruining their crop.

In this way, everything we come across is a hybridized plant, but that does not mean you can’t get products that will provide an “Indica” or “Sativa” effect. The magic that determines the effects of a cannabis plant are found in the trichomes—a characteristic that is not tied to the characteristics of plant structures and growth cycles.
Getting a plant that will produce the effects you want, while also having an ideal structure and grow-cycle, is the work of cannabis farmers. It’s hard work to dial it in. Be sure to enjoy it!
Choosing the Right Strain for You
Selecting the right cannabis strain depends on your individual needs and preferences. Here are some tips to help you decide:

items: Determine Your Goals: Your goals will guide you towards either Indica, Sativa, or a hybrid strain. *Individual results may vary.
Consider the Time of Day: Use Indica strains in the evening to relax and unwind, and Sativa strains during the day to stay alert and active.
Experiment with Hybrids: If you’re new to cannabis or looking for a balanced effect, try hybrid strains to see how they work for you.
Consult with Experts: Visit a dispensary and talk to knowledgeable staff who can recommend strains based on your needs and preferences.

data.text: A Word on Edibles

There is still a lot of work to be done on understanding how edibles produce an indica or sativa effect. When we smoke cannabis, the compounds in the plant are vaporized and enter our bloodstream through our lungs. When eaten, those same compounds can have a different effect, as they get processed through our digestive system. THC is going to be more relaxing and felt more in the body when eaten, because of how it changes after being processed through the liver.

As for the other compounds (there are over 400 we know about!), we don’t have enough research to definitively say that the same profile of compounds that produce a sativa experience when smoked will produce the same effect when eaten. What this means is that edibles are typically made in one of two ways.

The first way is that they are made with strain-specific cannabis oil. Some believe, through personal experience, that this is enough to impact the effects of an edible. The logic being, if you use oil from an indica plant, you will get a relaxing effect.

The other way edibles are made is by adding non-cannabis ingredients or adding additional cannabinoids that are thought to produce relaxing effects. For example, in certain markets it is common to find indica edibles that include things like melatonin or CBN (a cannabinoid thought to produce relaxing effects).

This is why, when it comes to edibles, it is important to read the ingredients listed on the packaging. You want to know exactly what you’re getting. Maybe there are ingredients you are looking to avoid, maybe you already know exactly what you are looking for, or maybe you are looking to try something new.
Conclusion

Understanding the differences between Indica and Sativa cannabis strains is essential for anyone navigating the modern cannabis market. In modern cannabis shops, they are terms used to describe effects. That might change down the road, but, as for today, when you go into a cannabis shop, products will be organized by their effects, and those effects will often be categorized by either Indica or Sativa.

These categories may not reflect the fullest definitions of the words, but they are a great place to start when speaking to your budtender about the kind of effects you are hoping to experience. Whether you prefer the relaxing effects of Indica, the energizing properties of Sativa, or the balanced experience of a hybrid, there’s a cannabis strain out there for you. Happy exploring!

data.text: FAQ: Indica vs Sativa
What are the main differences between Indica and Sativa?

Indica strains are generally known for their potentially relaxing and sedative effects, making them suitable for evening use. Sativa strains are typically more energizing and uplifting, suitable for daytime use, and often have higher THC content. Individual results may vary.
What is the difference between Landrace and Heirloom strains?

All heirlooms are landrace, but not all landrace are heirloom strains. Landrace strains are connected to the land and the growing conditions of that place. It’s the unique expression of a plant that results from the environmental and human factors that nurtured it. Heirlooms are created when those plants are taken elsewhere. The expression of that traditional plant in the new environment will be different than if it had been grown in the place in which it naturally evolved. These differences can include the physical structure of the plant as well as the chemistry it produces in the trichomes.
What are hybrid strains?
Hybrid strains are a crossbreed of Indica and Sativa plants, designed to provide a balance of effects. They can be Indica-dominant, Sativa-dominant, or balanced, depending on the desired effects.
How should I choose between Indica and Sativa?

Your choice should depend on the effects you are looking for and the time of day you plan to use it. Indica is better for relaxation and nighttime use, while Sativa is more suitable for daytime use and activities requiring energy and focus.
Can the same strain affect different people differently?

Yes, individual responses to cannabis can vary widely based on factors like genetics, tolerance, and the specific chemical composition of the strain. Everyone’s endocannabinoid system is unique, and consumers should expect a unique experience.
Is one strain better than the other for beginners?
Beginners might prefer starting with a balanced hybrid or an Indica-dominant strain, as these can provide a more manageable experience. However, personal preference plays a significant role.

data.text: Basic Cannabis Terminology
Let’s start with some basic cannabis terms to help get you up to speed.
Adult-use

Adult-use is a term used to describe cannabis and access to cannabis for adults (21+ in most places). The term is used to differentiate between medical use and recreational use for everyday wellness and fun.
Bud
A nickname for cannabis flower. It refers to the bulbous flowers that are dried, cured, and smoked.
Budtender
The person who serves you at a cannabis dispensary and helps guide you towards the right product. At our shops we call them Wellness Advisors.
Cannabinoids
A group of natural chemical compounds produced by the cannabis plant that give cannabis its range of physical and mental effects. THC and CBD are the two most common cannabinoids.
Cannabis
Cannabis, also called marijuana, pot, weed, and various other slang terms, is a unique plant that produces psychoactive effects.
CBD

Short for Cannabidiol, CBD is one of the primary cannabinoids found in cannabis along with THC. Unlike THC, CBD is clear-headed. Which makes it attractive to those who don't want to alter their mind state.
CBG

Short for Cannabigerol, CBG is a cannabinoid found in cannabis that has gained a lot of interest recently. CBG is not as common as THC or CBD. The medical potential of CBG is thought to be helpful with inflammation, glaucoma, and even slowing cancer from spreading.
CBN
Short for Cannabinol, CBN is another cannabinoid found in cannabis that is formed as THC degrades. It shows potential as a sleep aid and as a way to stimulate the appetite.
Clones

Clones are clippings from cannabis plants that are used as starter plants. They are identical genetic replicas from the plant they are taken from, they ensure the sex of the plant, and save time when compared to growing cannabis from seed.
Cola
Cola is the term for the main flowering cluster on a cannabis plant.
Concentrate

Concentrates are cannabis extracts made by concentrating the resinous oils of the plant. These products contain the concentrated profile of the plant’s cannabinoid and terpene content. These preparations offer you all the enjoyable aspects of cannabis, like its taste and the way it makes you feel, without the plant’s leaves and vegetation.
Cultivar

Another name for a cannabis strain. A plant variety that has been developed for cultivation using selective breeding is known as a cultivar. Different types of cannabis cultivars are bred to emphasize characteristics like their smell, flavor, and chemical profile.
Dab
A dab is the process of instantly vaporizing cannabis concentrates on a heated surface known as a nail or banger. The term dab and dabs may also refer to the raw extract itself.
Dispensary
A retail store location where you can access cannabis for medical or recreational purposes.
Distillate

A thick amber oil distilled from the cannabis plant. Distillate is a purified cannabis oil that strips the plant down to its most basic compounds, generally THC or CBD, removing impurities and flavors in the process. Distilling cannabis often purifies its cannabinoid profile down to a much narrower spectrum, highlighting only THC or CBD instead of a more complete, whole-plant profile.
Edibles
An edible is any food or beverage that’s been infused with highly concentrated cannabis extract.
Eighth
Short for 1/8th ounce, a standard weight that cannabis flower is sold in. 3.5 grams = 1/8th oz
Extract
Extracts are cannabis oil products that have been concentrated using hydrocarbon solvents like butane and CO2 to produce a rich amber oil.
Flower

The common form of cannabis is the dried flower. Its resinous, dried flowers contain the highest natural concentrations of cannabinoids like THC and CBD, the psychoactive compounds that give cannabis its effects like THC and CBD.
Smaller flowers are often referred to as popcorn buds (see POPCORN) and finely ground flower prepared for rolling joints is known as shake.
Hash
Hash, short for hashish, is a term for the concentration of the sticky resin glands that have been separated and collected by hand using screens.
Hemp
Hemp is cannabis without the THC, less than 0.3% according to law. Traditionally it was bred and used for its fibers. Today much of the world’s hemp crop is utilized for it’s high-CBD content.
Hybrid
A classification of cannabis genetics that feature both indica and sativa genetics. These cultivars offer a balance between relaxing and uplifting effects.
Indica

Varieties of cannabis originating in the mountainous regions that grow with a short, bushy stature and large, thick leaves. Indica plants have a shorter flowering cycle than their sativa counterparts and are generally appreciated for their deeply relaxing effects.
Joint
A cannabis cigarette. Ground cannabis rolled in a paper that is ready to be smoked.
Kief

A collection of the plant’s resin glands, known as trichomes. Kief falls off the plant when it is ground or handled which is why many grinders feature a kief screen that can be used to collect the kief for use later.
Liquid Live Resin

Liquid Live Resin (LLR) Crafted from premium fresh frozen flower, liquid live resin is a high-terpene, full-spectrum cannabis oil. The gentle extraction process preserves the full plant profile, delivering superior aroma, potency and flavor compared to distillates. Ready to use in vape form.
Nug
Short for nugget, Nug is a slang term for cannabis flowers because the bulbous buds resemble small nuggets, like a collection of a precious mineral. Also see BUD.
Oil
A sticky amber substance extracted from the cannabis plant that contains the resins of the plant, also called hash oil.
Papers
Short for rolling papers, papers are specialized thin paper wraps used to roll cannabis into joints and pre-rolls.
Popcorn

Popcorn is a nickname for small buds that form on the lower branches of the plant. It is typically sold at a discounted rate compared to the top-shelf buds harvested off the main branches of the plant and is a great option for people who like to roll their own joints or cook with cannabis.
Pre-rolls
Another word for a joint (see Joint), pre-rolls are pre-rolled cannabis cigarettes.
Recreational Use

Recreational use (see Adult-use) refers to cannabis consumption for pleasure. Unlike medical use, recreational use does not targeting specific medical ailments or symptoms though it may still produce therapeutic effects.
RSO

Short for Rick Simpson Oil, RSO, is a sticky concentrated cannabis oil that is typically consumed orally or applied directly to the skin. Cancer patient Rick Simpson used his homemade preparations to combat his own cancer which is why this type of product bares his name.
Sativa

Varieties of cannabis originating in warmer equatorial regions that grow tall and skinny in stature with long, thin leaves. Sativa strains have a longer flowering cycle than their Indica counterparts and are appreciated for their uplifting effects.
Shake
Flower is sold as buds that are commonly smoked or vaporized. Typically, flower is sold in three varieties: fuller-sized buds, popcorn buds that are smaller in size, and shake–which is loose flower.
Strain

A strain is a unique genetic variety of cannabis. Each time cannabis strains are bred together to create a new variety a new strain of cannabis is born. A few popular examples of strains are Blue Dream, Sour Diesel, and Northern Lights. Also see Cultivar.
THC
Tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, is the primary psychoactive compound that cannabis produces. It is known for producing euphoric effects .
Terpene

Terpenes are a diverse group of organic compounds produced by plants. Terpenes give cannabis its variety of aromas and flavors as well as modulate the effects of cannabinoids like THC and CBD by working together in what’s known as the entourage effect. Common terpenes include: Myrcene (also found in mangoes), Caryophyllene (also found in cracked pepper) Linalool (also found in lavender), and Pinene (also found in rosemary).
Tincture
Tinctures are liquid cannabis elixirs that can be taken orally or easily added to food and drinks.
Trichome

Translucent mushroom-shaped glands on the cannabis plant that are sticky to the touch and give it its frosted white appearance. Barely visible to the human eye, these small hair-like glands produce and store the essential oils of cannabis that contain the cannabinoids and terpenes responsible for the flavors and effects of cannabis.
Topical

Cannabis topicals are products like creams and lotions that are infused with cannabis and applied directly to your skin. They are often used for sore muscles, inflammation, and localized pain management.
Vape

Cannabis vapes are a popular and simple way to consume cannabis oil easily and discreetly. Vapes are prefilled vaporizer cartridges or pods. When paired with a battery these small devices allow you to vaporize cannabis concentrates without combusting the plant. They come preloaded with various types of cannabis oil and allow you to enjoy cannabis at the push of a button. Vapes are fast-acting, discreet, easy-to-use, and make dosing simple. data.text: It certainly goes without saying that being a parent isn’t easy. Some cannabis consumers seek stress reduction, while others look to restore balance in their everyday lives (individual results may vary). Fitting cannabis into your daily lifestyle isn’t off limits simply because you’re also raising a family. While public attitudes toward cannabis are quickly evolving, there’s a lingering stigma around using cannabis if you happen to also be a parent. Let’s have a look at the best practices around responsible cannabis use and the community support for consumers with kids.
Breaking stigmas around cannabis and parenting

Mainstream cannabis acceptance is at an all-time high: 91% of U.S. adults support legal medical and recreational programs, and 25% of Americans now regularly consume cannabis. It’s also worth noting that since 2021, 44% of cannabis-consuming parents with children under 18 tried it for the first time, and 62% of parents who consume cannabis believe celebrating 420 has become more acceptable.* Around the U.S., parents and adults are finding ways to incorporate cannabis into their everyday occasions.

When used responsibly, the reported effects of cannabis can be calming, creative, relaxing, or amusing (individual results may vary). For regular consumers, their regimen of THC or CBD-laden products may factor into overall feelings of relaxation, which is something parents often say they need more of. In addition, some adults say they substitute drinking alcohol for an infused cannabis product or beverage to avoid lingering effects the next morning (individual results may vary).
Maintaining a safe environment when storing and consuming cannabis

“I also love to use cannabis edibles after my kids go to bed and I have a few moments of peace to watch a show, catch up on texts, read, and know I have a deeper sleep ahead of me,” said cannabis professional and mother, Lane.

If you are living with children in your home or have children visiting your home, it’s critical to practice safe cannabis usage and storage, as well as making sure any consumption is not in close physical proximity to anyone under 21 years of age. Responsible consumption in a household with minors means:

items: Always keeping cannabis products in their original, child-resistant packaging.
Ensuring cannabis products are properly resealed and stored in their child-resistant packaging after each and every use.
Always storing cannabis products in a high cabinet, drawer or cupboard that is also locked and out of the reach of children.
Not taking a dose that would significantly impair parental responsibilities. Start low, go slow—microdose to start out.

Know Your Limits

Every Sunnyside market has its own set of rules when it comes to how much cannabis you can buy—and those limits can vary based on whether you're a medical patient or an adult-use (recreational) shopper, and whether you're a resident or just visiting. To make things easier, we've broken down the legal purchase limits for each state we serve. These tables include both medical and recreational allowances, where applicable, along with in-state and out-of-state guidelines if they differ.

Illinois medical cardholders can use that card to purchase cannabis in Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico, DC, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Maine, according to the ILDPH. And in Utah, Oklahoma, Hawaii, Georgia, and Arkansas, you need to apply for a 'medical cannabis visitor card' in order to use your Illinois medical card in those states. Check your state's regulations online for more detailed information.

data.alt: Illinois Medical and Recreational Marijuana Purchasing Limits

data.text: In Illinois, medical purchases are tracked on a rolling 14-day period (2.5oz flower max). Recreational purchase limits apply per day, with separate allowances for in-state and out-of-state shoppers.

In Florida, medical cannabis purchases are tracked over 35- or 70-day periods (smokable: 2.5 oz per 35 days, max 4 oz possession; inhalation/vaporized: 24,500 mg THC; oral: 14,000 mg THC; edibles: 4,200 mg THC; sublingual: 13,300 mg THC; topical: 10,500 mg THC). Patients may request an exemption to increase their allotment.

In Massachusetts, medical limits are based on a 60-day supply (usually up to 10oz flower). Recreational limits are applied per day and per transaction, and are the same for all adults regardless of residency. 56g of flower OR dry flower equivalent in edibles (1000mg) or oil (10g). Massachusetts enforces a daily recreational limit but a longer period rolling cap for medical use.

In Pennsylvania, if no limit is set by your physician, a '90-day supply' is equivalent to 192 medical marijuana units. One (1) unit is equivalent to 3.5 grams of flower, 1 gram of concentrate, or 100 milligrams of THC infused into a pill, capsule, oil, liquid, tincture or topical form.
*In Ohio, Medical patients (excluding caregivers) can also buy up to a 4-day supply at once—equal to 10 ounces of flower and 60,000 mg of THC.

data.alt: New York Medical and Recreational Marijuana Purchasing Limits

data.text: In New York, medical limits vary based on the practitioner's recommendation (typically a 30-day supply). Recreational limits apply per possession rather than per transaction or per day, and there's no distinction between in-state and out-of-state shoppers.

What does 420 mean?
“420” is a widely recognized slang term for cannabis. It can refer to:

items: The time of day (4:20 PM) to consume cannabis
A general reference to marijuana use
The date April 20th (4/20), now a global cannabis holiday

data.text: Today, the term is deeply embedded in cannabis culture and is used casually to signal cannabis-friendly attitudes, events, and communities.
Where Did 420 Come From?

The origin of 420 dates back to 1971 in San Rafael, California. A group of five high school students—nicknamed “The Waldos”—would meet at 4:20 PM after school to search for a rumored hidden cannabis crop. While the treasure was never found, the ritual stuck. “420” became their code word for smoking, and over time, the phrase spread beyond their circle—eventually becoming a universal symbol for cannabis culture.
Why Is 420 Associated With Marijuana?
420 became associated with marijuana through word-of-mouth, cultural adoption, and media exposure.
What started as a private joke evolved into:

items: A daily ritual time (4:20 PM)
A shared language among cannabis users
A cultural identifier for cannabis-friendly spaces

title: Supporting Mission [Green]
description: Learn how Sunnyside is supporting Mission Green; furthering justice reform for those who are incarcerated—and what you can do to help.

data.text: Black History Month is one opportunity to celebrate Black stories.

In 2025, we partnered with The Weldon Project through the Mission [Green] Initiative to help them right the wrongs of the War on Drugs, especially those in the Black community who were and are disproportionately affected by it. Even though Black and White people consume cannabis at similar rates, historically, Black people are 4 times more likely to be arrested and more likely to get harsher punishment. [1, 2] We believe in keeping that conversation going all year, but it’s certainly on our minds during Black History Month.

Last year, we raised over $55,000 through corporate donations and across our 10 stores in Illinois with round-ups. This year, we're proud to kick off our partnership with an in-store round-up program to our 31 stores in Florida from February 4th-28th, in addition to our donation.

The Mission [Green] Initiative is powered by The Weldon Project, a nonprofit organization that dedicates resources to fund social change and provide financial assistance to those serving non-violent cannabis-related sentences. The Mission [Green] Initiative works to provide commissary and clemency programs that help these individuals.

With our donations, the Mission [Green] Hand Up program provides commissary financial assistance to incarcerated individuals for basic care items like food and hygiene products. Our support helps these individuals  feel less isolated and more supported, reinforcing that someone on the outside cares for them.

Mission [Green] also works as advocates for these individuals to create pathways to pardons or expungements. Their  initiative has developed a proclamation for justice with support from Democratic and Republican leaders, as well as from prominent figures in the sports and entertainment industries.

The Weldon Project and Mission [Green] were founded by Weldon Angelos, a rising star in the music industry, whose career was cut short when he was sentenced to a mandatory 55 years in federal prison for selling $300 of cannabis on three occasions.

In 2016 – after an unprecedented, bipartisan campaign to secure his freedom by elected and appointed government officials, celebrities, advocates, business leaders, and various media outlets – Angelos was finally released from prison after serving 13 years for a first-time, cannabis-related offense. In December of 2020, he was fully pardoned by President Trump.

Now that Weldon is free, he is working to reclaim his life while fighting to end marijuana prohibition, the war on drugs, and mass incarceration. Thousands of people are still lingering in federal and state prisons across the country serving outdated, cannabis-related sentences, but our contributions provide meaningful hope and support to those still incarcerated.

title: How to Pack and Smoke the Perfect Bowl
description: Smoking a bowl is one of the most iconic ways to consume cannabis. The method for packing a bowl is simple, but similar to rolling a joint, there are a few steps you can take to elevate the overall enjoyability of the experience. Here’s what you need to know to pack and hit a bowl perfectly.

data.text: Smoking a bowl is one of the most iconic ways to consume cannabis. The method for packing a bowl is simple, but similar to rolling a joint, there are a few steps you can take to elevate the overall enjoyability of the experience. Here’s what you need to know to pack and hit a bowl perfectly.
What is a bowl?

A bowl is the part of a pipe that holds the cannabis. Unlike the bowl you use for your breakfast cereal, this has a small hole at the bottom so smoke can make its way through the pipe. “Smoking a bowl” is a common term used by cannabis consumers to smoke a pipe. Bowls come in a variety of shapes and sizes, but most are designed to hold less than a gram of flower . For larger pipes or bongs, the bowl can be removed from the rest of the pipe when it’s time to pack or needs to be cleaned . There are pipes that have bowls built in, but they are typically smaller pieces (spoon pipes or bubblers). They function similarly, but they’re harder to clean—and one wrong move can render the entire pipe useless if it breaks. For bongs, the bowl slides into the downstem. The downstem creates a seal through the water, which allows the smoke to build up in the main chamber of your piece. When you want to clear the chamber, just slide the bowl out and inhale through the mouthpiece of the bong. Pipes that have a built-in bowl rely on a carb (short for carburetor) to function. The carb is a second hole that sits on the side of the bowl. When you light the bowl, you put your thumb over the carb to create a seal. When you want to clear the chamber, simply remove your thumb and continue to inhale through the end of the pipe.
How to pack a bowl
Gather what you need to pack a bowl
• Cannabis : Cannabis flower is going to provide the base of the bowl. You can also add a topper like kief or an extract to up the potency and flavor.

• Grinder: Grinders are typically circular tools used to break down cannabis. They come in various materials—metal, plastic, and wood. The most common style is the four-piece metal grinder, consisting of a lid with grinding teeth, a grind section with holes for weed to fall through, a storage chamber with a screen for filtering kief, and a kief catcher at the bottom.
• Pipe / Bong: A device used to consume cannabis. Cannabis is packed in the bowl.

• Screen (optional): Placed at the bottom of the bowl, a screen keeps small cannabis particulates from making their way through the pipe. This will help keep pipes cleaner and help consumers avoid getting cannabis material in their mouths.
• Tamping Tool (optional): A tool used to help pack the cannabis flower into the bowl. This will ensure a smooth and even burn.
• Poker: A tool that is used to clear the used cannabis material from the bowl. It can also be used to help clear resin from clogging the hole at the bottom of the bowl.

• Lighter / Hemp Wick / Herb Iron: Whatever you use to combust your cannabis. Lighters are most common, but some people prefer to use hemp wick or an herb iron to preserve the flavor of their cannabis.

data.alt: Cannabis, grinder, bowl, tamping tool, poker, and lighter — these are common tools and accessories to pack and smoke a bowl of marijuana.

data.text: Break down your cannabis

Whole cannabis flowers do not burn well, so the first thing you’ll need to do is break down your cannabis. The goal is consistency with the size. This is why using a grinder is so helpful—it’ll do that work for you. Just put your flower in the grinding chamber and twist. If you don’t have a grinder, you can break down your flower with your hands or a pair of small, sharp scissors.
Fill the bowl

Once you’re done grinding, start filling the bowl a little at a time. Some grinders have a chamber that will nicely hold the cannabis for you. If your grinder does not have a chamber for the ground flower, use a small tray to hold your cannabis. As you fill the bowl, gently tamp down the cannabis with either your thumb or a tamping tool. Packing a bowl too lightly will have the cannabis burn up too quickly and possibly produce a harsh smoking experience. If you pack it too tight, you can clog the bowl and create a difficult draw.
Expert bowl packing tips

• Break down the cannabis into a consistent size. This will ensure that the flower burns evenly and you get a smooth smoke. Stems and seeds should also be removed from the mix before breaking down the cannabis. You can smoke stems and seeds, but they add nothing to the experience.

• Pack firmly and don’t over pack the bowl. Overpacking the bowl can create a difficult draw on the pipe. Packing loosely will also create problems for smoking. The perfectly packed bowl will create a beautiful draw and a tasty smoke. A well-packed bowl will also often stay lit after your session. This is why it is courteous to extinguish the fire with a tamping tool (or bottom of your lighter) after you finish your inhale.

• Add concentrates to up potency and flavor. After the flower has been packed, you can top the bowl with kief or concentrate to enhance the enjoyment. Be mindful that concentrates will burn differently than flower.

data.alt: A cannabis grinder, tray, and bowl are used to pack a bowl, minimizing additional messes.

data.text: How to smoke a bowl

Before you smoke, make sure that your finger is over the carb or the bowl is securely in the down stem of your bong. Hold the pipe with one hand, and with your other hand, slowly bring the flame to the edge of the bowl. As you begin to inhale, the flame will catch the flower. At that point, you can put down the flame. The flower will stay lit and the chamber of your pipe will begin to fill. Remove your finger from the carb or the bowl from the down stem when you’re ready to inhale the smoke from the chamber.
Bowl smoking techniques

Smoking cannabis can be a communal activity. When smoking with friends, it’s common courtesy to preserve some “greens” for them. In other words, if the plan is to share the bowl and you go first, don’t light the entire bowl and scorch all the flower. This kills all the flavor and potency for the next person. Make sure your friend has something green to smoke when you hand it over. If there’s none left, finish the bowl and pack another. It’s only polite! This is the proper technique used to help preserve “greens” in a bowl. Instead of lighting the entire bowl on fire, simply bring the flame close to the edge of the bowl and begin to inhale. Your breath will draw the flame into the flower. Instead of scorching all the cannabis, it will burn a section of the flower (like a slice of pizza). This will ensure when you pass the pipe, your friend will have a tasty hit. When all the cannabis has been consumed, remove the ash from the bowl. Most of it will come out with a gentle tap, but a poker can be helpful in getting any leftover material that wants to stick around. You’re then ready for your next bowl. Once you get the rhythm down, packing a bowl becomes second nature. It can even become a cherished ritual you use to unwind.

FAQ
What's the difference between a pipe and a bong?

A pipe is a handheld piece with a built-in bowl and a carb hole you cover while inhaling. A bong is a larger pipe that uses water to filter and cool the smoke. Bongs usually have a removable bowl that slides into a downstem.
How much weed should I pack in a bowl?
Most bowls hold less than a gram of flower. For solo sessions, a light to medium pack (about 0.25–0.5g) is usually plenty. Larger bongs or party bowls can hold more.
Should I use a screen in my bowl?
A screen is optional, but it helps keep ash and small particles from being pulled through the pipe. It also keeps your pipe cleaner for longer.
How fine should I grind my weed?
Grind your cannabis to a medium consistency—not powdery, but small enough to allow air to pass evenly through the bowl. Too fine, and it clogs; too coarse, and it burns unevenly.
How tightly should I pack the bowl?
Pack your bowl firmly but not too tight. You want airflow for a smooth draw. Overpacking restricts airflow; underpacking burns too quickly and harshly.
What's the best way to light a bowl?
Use a lighter, hemp wick, or herb iron, and aim the flame toward the edge of the bowl instead of the center. This “slicing” technique preserves fresh flower (“greens”) for the next person.
What does 'saving the greens' mean?
It’s smoking etiquette —when sharing, you light only part of the bowl so others can enjoy unburned flower with full flavor and potency.
How do I know when the bowl is finished?
When there’s no more smoke and the material turns gray or white ash, the bowl is cashed. Tap it gently or use a poker to clear it out before repacking.
How do I clean my bowl?

Remove any leftover ash, then soak your pipe or bong parts in isopropyl alcohol and coarse salt. Shake gently, rinse thoroughly, and let dry completely before using again. Check out our blog on how to thoroughly clean your glassware.
Can I mix concentrates or kief in my bowl?
Absolutely. Sprinkling a bit of kief or concentrate on top adds potency and flavor.

title: Enjoying Music Festivals and Cannabis
description:
Music festival season is a rite of passage for summer: seeing a once-in-a-lifetime combination of bands while moving alongside thousands of fellow fans, there’s an energy to the live experience that can’t be replicated anywhere else. 

We're here to remind you how to stay safe while you enjoy cannabis this festival season!

data.text: There's no disputing that cannabis has influenced countless creative pursuits in music. From Wiz Khalifa to Willie Nelson to Miley Cyrus, cannabis culture has crossed over to multiple genres. If you're planning on attending a music festival this summer, you may be wondering how you can enjoy an elevated experience while keeping yourself and your friends safe and in compliance with the venue's consumption policies. As always, find out the locality and festival's policies for on-site consumption and possession of cannabis before you leave home - even if your state has legalized cannabis for recreational use, enforcement will differ from venue to venue. For more ways to elevate your next concert experience, here are some tips for pairing cannabis and live music.

data.text: Why Music and Cannabis Pair Perfectly

On top of the cultural connection between cannabis and music, there's a case to be made that consuming THC while listening to your favorite artists makes the vibe even better. While individual results may vary, some of the reported effects of cannabis - like altered sound and time perception - harmonize with the auditory experience of a live music environment. There's also the growing trend of concert attendees choosing cannabis over alcohol, not only as a lifestyle choice, but because taking an edible or a hitting a vape is easier than safeguarding a beer or cocktail in a crowd. For those attending a multi-day festival, replacing your alcohol intake with cannabis also helps ensure you don't have a lingering hangover that could impact tomorrow's lineup.

data.alt: Sunnyside vape pens held in the air

data.text: Good advice for festivals:
1. Plan Ahead

If you want to consume cannabis at a festival, you should understand your tolerance and consumption preferences so you don't overdo it. You should also research the festival's cannabis policies before you go, and if activities like tailgating or on-site consumption are allowed.
2. Start Low & Go Slow

If you plan on using edibles, start low until you understand your ideal dose—keeping in mind that you can always consume more, but you can't consume less. Same goes for vapes; you can always take small hits throughout a set rather than finding yourself in the deep end off too big a hit.
3. Pack Smart

Starting with your clothes and gear, your festival experience can sink or swim based on whether you have the proper essentials. Make sure to drink plenty of water and pack sunglasses, sunscreen, earplugs, and comfortable shoes so you can bounce from stage to stage. A rag you can soak to cool off never hurt anyone either!
4. Hydrate, Hydrate, Hydrate

Festivals get hot! Between walking outside, dancing all day, and limited shade coverage, it's critical to drink plenty of water. When you sweat, you not only lose water, but you also lose electrolytes like sodium and potassium. Keep your water supply topped up throughout the day, not just for you but for your friends. And in the event of cannabis overconsumption, stay calm, drink plenty of water and rest in a shady spot while waiting for things to pass.
5. Have A Buddy

Music festivals often take place at venues hosting thousands of people-often with spotty cell phone reception and Wi-Fi signals. You and a buddy should organize a central meeting place in the unfortunate event that you're separated in a crowd.
6. Don't Overdo It

Remember that all-day or multi-day music festivals are meant to be enjoyed, not a contest for who can consume the most. Taking care of the little details like dressing right, wearing ear plugs, and taking breaks will go a long way towards a sustainable experience.
7. Buy Safe

Only state-licensed dispensaries offer rigorously lab-tested products, so you can trust that they're not contaminated with impurities. That's not the case with unlicensed shops and illicit market dealers. Since they're unregulated, you might be buying products that have mold, pesticide, or bacterial contamination-and even other harmful substances like lead, arsenic or dangerous additives. Worse, some products may contain far less or far more THC than advertised-leading to a potentially unpleasant experience. Every cannabis product at a licensed dispensary is responsibly-dosed and has lab testing results displayed prominently on the label, so you know exactly what you're buying and consuming. title: What is CBD, and what does it do?
description: CBD, short for cannabidiol, is a naturally-occurring compound found in the cannabis plant.

data.text: CBD, short for cannabidiol, is a naturally-occurring compound found in the cannabis plant. Unlike THC, CBD is non-psychoactive, meaning it won’t get you “high.” Which is exactly why it has become such a popular option for those wanting to explore the potential benefits of cannabis.
In this guide, you’ll discover everything you need to know about CBD—from how it works to the different types of products available, and even how it compares to other cannabinoids.
What does CBD do?

CBD interacts with your endocannabinoid system (ECS)—a vast network of receptors in your brain and body that helps regulate mood, pain, sleep, appetite, and immune response. Unlike THC, which binds directly to receptors (especially CB1 in the brain), CBD works alongside the naturally-occurring cannabinoids in your body to maintain balance. Although we still don’t fully understand how CBD works, and the exact mechanisms are still being studied, researchers believe CBD may encourage the body to use its own natural endocannabinoids more effectively.
What are CBD products?

Similar to THC , CBD is a naturally occurring compound in the cannabis plant. It is incredibly versatile and can be found in a variety of formats. Each product type serves different preferences and needs. Here’s a list of the ways that CBD can be consumed:

items: CBD Flower: Some people prefer to go directly to the source. Cannabis flower can be CBD dominant (not just hemp), with only trace elements of THC. So, if you prefer the experience of smoking a joint or a bowl and are still looking to avoid the psychoactive effects of THC, you have an option.

CBD Oil & Vapes: Whether it's vaped or dabbed (deconstructed vaping), CBD oil is quickly becoming the preferred product for those that want to feel the effects of their CBD immediately. In addition to being fast-acting, vapes can also be very discreet, as they are small and produce minimal odor.

CBD Edibles: Gummies, chocolates, capsules, and  beverages offer a tasty, discreet way to consume CBD. Unlike smoking or vaping, edibles can take a while for the effects to kick in. Depending on a variety of factors, you should expect to feel the effects anywhere between 20 and 40 minutes (individual results may vary). Edibles are also really easy to store and have a longer shelf-life than flower.

CBD Tinctures: Tinctures are infused liquids that are taken under the tongue for fast absorption. So, instead of having to process through the entire gut system, the cannabinoids can enter the bloodstream directly. If you're looking to avoid smoking or vaporization, and you want something more fast-acting than an edible, a CBD tincture may be right for you.

CBD Topicals: Creams and lotions applied directly to the skin for localized effects. Most of these products will not enter the bloodstream; however, some products are designed to be transdermal—meaning they have added compounds to help them get through the skin and into your bloodstream. Be mindful of this, as transdermal creams will provide all-over effects instead of localized.

data.text: What is full-spectrum CBD?

CBD can be formulated in full-spectrum, broad-spectrum, or isolate forms, and CBD products are made from all three of these forms. Full-Spectrum CBD In short, “full-spectrum” means “true to the plant.” It means that effort was taken in the extraction process to make sure that the hundreds of compounds (cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids, etc.) that are found in the cannabis flower made their way into the oil.

When it comes to quality, full-spectrum is the pinnacle of cannabis oils because it is where you get the most dynamic entourage effect . The effects are more robust, they last longer, and may provide a more enjoyable experience (individual results may vary). Broad-Spectrum CBD Similar to full-spectrum, but these are lacking a few compounds that are found in the original plant material. Sometimes this is done on purpose. For example, occasionally producers want to completely eliminate THC from their oil (full-spectrum CBD oils will typically have a small amount of THC).

Other times, the extraction process is unable to capture the full-spectrum of compounds or the starting material used to create the oil is not the freshest or highest quality. Many of the compounds in cannabis are extremely volatile, and they will disappear in a few months—even if stored properly. So, if a producer wants to process mid-level cannabis, it makes more sense for them to use an extraction method that is faster and produces higher yields of cannabinoids.
Broad-spectrum oil can still be considered high quality and may offer desirable effects. It just depends on the extraction method and the starting material.

CBD Isolate Isolates produce the eye-popping percentage numbers on the packaging; however, they lack the other properties that make cannabis cannabis. Products with CBD isolate are best for people who want a focused CBD experience or are avoiding THC entirely. They can be consumed by themselves, or they can be added to more full-spectrum products to infuse more CBD into the experience.
What’s nice about isolates is that they're easy and cost-effective to make for producers, so you can get a lot of CBD for your money.

data.text: What is CBD used for?

CBD has rapidly become a go-to wellness option for people seeking natural alternatives to traditional medications. It's typically used by people that want the potential benefits of cannabis without the psychoactive component of the experience. It was originally only found in cannabis shops, but you can now easily find it in products at your grocery store and within major cosmetic lines.
Is CBD legal?

In the United States, CBD derived from hemp (defined as cannabis with less than 0.3% THC) was federally legalized under the 2018 Farm Bill. However, CBD derived from marijuana (plants containing more than 0.3% THC) remains a Schedule I substance under federal law. This is an odd way to structure the legality of CBD (hemp is marijuana and there is no way to determine what kind of plant your CBD was derived from), but this is pretty standard for cannabis laws in general—confusing. The main takeaway here is that THC remains federally illegal. If you’re a farmer, don’t grow it. If you’re a consumer in states where cannabis is illegal, don’t have it in your possession.

This federal legalization meant that for many people living in the United States, they would now have access to CBD. Even if cannabis wasn’t legal in their state, they could get CBD products mailed to them. Key Legal Points:

items: Hemp-derived CBD is federally legal.
State laws vary , and some states regulate or restrict CBD sales.
Always check local regulations before purchasing or using CBD products.

data.text: CBD and Epilepsy

The last decade has seen the legalization of cannabis take massive strides forward, and, even though it's not federally legal, there's still cause for celebration. It's also important to remember what helped push this movement forward. CBD is one of those things.

Up until the release of CNN’s documentary “Weed,” most people did not truly understand the potential benefits of cannabis, let alone feel the need to fight for legal access to it. Cannabis still carried with it all the cultural baggage of drugs like heroin or cocaine, so the fight was more than just exploring the potential health benefits. Cannabis needed to be seen in a different light.

In “Weed,” the world got a glimpse of a little girl (Charlotte Figi) in a battle for her life with a severe seizure disorder (Dravet syndrome). After modern medicine offered no relief, her parents explored alternative methods. The documentary shows how CBD cannabis oil was able to drastically decrease the number of seizures Charlotte was experiencing (300 a week) so that she could have a childhood. It became clear that cannabis legalization was more than just a clever ploy by hippies to get high legally.

Since the federal legalization of hemp-derived CBD, one of the most researched uses of CBD is in the treatment of seizures. In 2018, the FDA approved Epidiolex, a CBD-based drug, for managing Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and Dravet syndrome, two rare and severe forms of epilepsy. This was a groundbreaking moment for CBD and helped legitimize its potential to a skeptical public.

It’s no coincidence that medical cannabis markets began to open across the nation after this shift in perception, and it’s no coincidence that the recreational market was always close behind. Once the cultural baggage was set aside, people finally got to see what cannabis really was—a beautiful plant.
What's the difference between CBD and THC?

CBD and THC are two of the most well-known cannabinoids, but they have very different potential effects. While THC binds directly to brain receptors to potentially uplift mood, CBD does not cause intoxication and is favored by those seeking the potential benefits of cannabis without altered mental states:
What is CBD vs CBG?

CBG (cannabigerol) is often called the “mother cannabinoid” because it’s the chemical precursor to other cannabinoids. While CBD is classified as a major cannabinoid because it can be found in abundance in cannabis, CBG is a minor cannabinoid because it’s only found in small amounts.

CBG isn't always a beneficial presence on the production side of cannabis. For example, a cannabis farmer may not want to find CBG in their plant at harvest, because it means they harvested too early and the plant didn’t have time to convert it into THC or CBD. If THC and CBD were the goal, CBG just means lost opportunity; however, those hoping to enhance the entourage effect of their product might find it useful.
While research is still developing, both compounds may offer potential benefits and might be even more effective when used together, thanks to the entourage effect.
Final Thoughts

CBD is a fast-growing option that may offer potential benefits for those looking to use cannabis without the psychoactive effects. As with any supplement, it's important to choose high-quality, lab-tested products and speak with a healthcare provider to ensure it’s right for you. Enjoy! (Individual results may vary).
FAQs about CBD
Does CBD get you high?
No. CBD is non-intoxicating and does not produce a euphoric “high” like THC.
Is CBD safe?
CBD is generally considered safe and well-tolerated. However, it can interact with certain medications, so consult your doctor before starting.
How long does CBD take to work?
It depends on the delivery method. Oils may work within 15–30 minutes, while edibles can take up to 1–2 hours.
Will I fail a drug test using CBD?
Pure CBD isolate won’t trigger a positive result. However, full-spectrum products contain trace THC and may show up on a test.

data.text: What is an edible?

Cannabis edibles are products which are infused with cannabis. Most edibles you see will be infused with THC and CBD , but other cannabinoids like CBG, CBN , and CBC are starting to make their way onto the shelves of cannabis shops. These cannabinoids are extracted from the cannabis plant and that oil is then incorporated into various products, such as chocolates, gummies, cookies, beverages, and more. That sounds simple enough, but there's more to making edibles than just mixing cannabis with other edible ingredients.
How are cannabis edibles made?

It's important to understand that cannabis plants don't produce active cannabinoids that will get you high. They produce THCa , which is non-psychoactive. It's only after THCa is heated that it turns into THC and becomes psychoactive. That's why we smoke cannabis to get its effects, and it is also why simply eating raw cannabis will not produce a psychoactive experience.

For a cannabis edible to produce a psychoactive effect, the cannabis needs to be heated. This can happen before the cannabis is incorporated into a recipe, or it can happen during the cooking process. The scientific name for this process is decarboxylation, but it is often shortened to "decarb" in the cannabis community.

The second challenge that faces cannabis edible makers is that cannabis oil isn't water soluble-it needs a fat to bind to. That's why many edible producers will infuse an oil or butter before they mix it in with the other ingredients. This ensures that the cannabinoids get evenly distributed throughout the recipe-giving the maker the ability to determine dosage.

Yes, you can simply put activated cannabis into a recipe, and it will get you high. The issues start to happen when you want to make a batch with multiple servings. It only takes a small amount of cannabis oil to infuse a large batch of baked goods. If the active ingredients in that oil have nothing to bind to, they will remain isolated from the other ingredients and won't distribute evenly throughout the entire batch.

This means that one edible can have all of the oil, and the rest have none. Instead of 24 nicely dosed cookies, you have 23 regular cookies and one super cookie that will probably get you more elevated than you would have liked. This is a common reason why many people have horror stories about taking a homemade edible. Take the time to infuse a single ingredient—an ingredient that will easily and evenly distribute itself throughout the batch—before mixing everything together to ensure better experiences.

This is also why it took a while for cannabis-infused beverages to get to market. In order to make cannabis beverages work, the water and cannabis oil need to get nano-emulsified. In other words, the water is not actually getting infused, but the water and oil molecules get broken down to such small pieces that the surface tension between the molecules is strong enough to keep themselves separate. All you have to do is make sure the beverage gets a good shake before dosing it out, and you're good to go!

data.text: Smoking and eating cannabis both rely on decarboxylation to work; however, they are going to produce vastly different experiences. When you smoke cannabis, you feel the effects of the THC immediately, as the active compounds are brought directly to your bloodstream through your lungs.

Edibles are different. Before they get to your bloodstream, they need to take a ride through your digestive system, and that takes time! How quickly you experience the effects depends upon a few things. Is there anything else in your stomach? How quick is your body processing food? Regardless of what you've consumed before, or the unique nature of your body chemistry, most people will start to feel the effects between 30 minutes and an hour. (Individual results may vary)

Some edibles are designed to take effect more quickly. Liquid edibles will take effect quicker than solid edibles, as they are more easily absorbed. Tinctures are designed to be absorbed directly into your bloodstream sublingually-avoiding the lengthy trip through your system altogether. Just put a few drops under your tongue and wait.

Dosage

Many edibles will be dosed out to 10mgs (5mgs for Massachusetts adult-use customers), but, considering that everyone is going to have a unique tolerance, that doesn't mean that's how much you should take. For some, 10mgs is going to be the perfect dosage. For others, 10mgs can be not enough to feel any effects whatsoever or be too much and overwhelming. Experience is the only way you're going to determine what your ideal dose will be, so start low and take it slow.

For beginners, it might be wise to start with 2.5mgs or 5mgs. Given the delayed onset of edibles, you'll then want to wait at least 2 hours before you take another dose. This will give you enough time to determine your tolerance and make adjustments.

Are there different types of weed edibles?

Most edibles are going to be made with cannabis extracts, and, similar to vaporizing, different extracts are going to produce different effects. Here's a brief breakdown of the different extracts you'll find in edibles:
Distillate

The most common extract used in edibles and vapes. Distillate is inexpensive to process and produces the highest THC percentages, but it lacks the diversity of compounds of other extracts. It is essentially just isolated THC. This creates an experience that is less complex and short lived-in vapes and edibles. It's extra convenient for edibles because the process to create it involves heat and produces an oil that is already activated, and it won't produce a "weedy" taste.
